items.title: Using Lunar Craters as Free Radiation Shields for Moon Base Nuclear Reactors
items.blurb: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the Moon. A new paper from researchers at Los Alamos, NASA Glenn, Oak Ridge, Idaho National Lab, and Lockheed Martin, and presented at the American Nuclear Society’s Nuclear and Emerging Technologies for Space (NETS) conference back in April, offers a simple solution to one major problem for any such future nuclear reactor - shielding.

items.title: Comet Encke's Shape and Heat Revealed in Thermal Glow

While comets primarily orbit in the farthest reaches of the solar system, specifically the Kuiper Belt or Oort Cloud, some make their way closer to the Sun. When this happens, the increased heat cause cometary icy material to evaporate, producing a spectacular tail while also revealing the rocky material underneath, known as a comet’s nucleus. But how well can astronomers use telescopic observations to study the composition and temperatures of a cometary nucleus?

Of the three, dark energy remains challenging because it's driving the acceleration of the expanding Universe. However, we can't see it, or even put a description to it, other than, "it's mysterious".

items.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
items.blurb: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

items.title: A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space
items.blurb: Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars spread heavy elements into space with their stellar winds. This material eventually forms more stars, and even rocky planets like ours. For a long time, astronomers thought this important mass-loss was driven by stellar winds. But new research shows how magnetic fields play an important role. A vast flare and magnetic loop of material from the AGB star Mira provides the evidence.

items.title: Webb Reveals New Details in Supernova Remnant

items.title: Euclid breaks own quasar record by 40 million years
items.blurb: The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope has discovered the most distant quasar to date: a rare 360 million-sun-mass galactic core seen just 630 million years after the Big Bang. The discovery breaks Euclid’s own previous record, announced only a few months ago[1.1], by peering back in time an additional 40 million years. It also raises a compelling question: how could such an enormous black hole have formed and grown so rapidly after the Big Bang?

items.title: BepiColombo safely in Mercury orbit despite unexpected challenge
items.blurb: On 21 November, starting at 18:24 UTC, BepiColombo achieved Mercury orbit insertion (MOI), the second major milestone of its planetary arrival phase. As soon as the signal from the spacecraft was re-established after a scheduled loss of contact, the Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, saw that the spacecraft had entered safe mode. An issue occurred during the thruster burn, causing the manoeuvre to end earlier than expected. Since then, teams at ESOC have been working around the clock with lead spacecraft manufacturer Airbus and colleagues across the joint ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission to investigate the issue, which has been traced to a software glitch. BepiColombo is safe and in a stable orbit around Mercury – an important milestone after its eight-year journey to the planet – and is on track for the separation of its two science orbiters on 9 December in Germany (10 December in Japan). The mission also delivered a first: entering orbit around another planet using ‘weak stability capture’. This involves arriving at lower speeds than is typical for planetary missions, and is a technique that has previously only been used by some spacecraft travelling to Earth's moon.

items.title: Shared membrane protects tuberculosis bacteria from antibiotics
items.blurb: Tuberculosis ranks among the world's deadliest infectious diseases. More than 1.1 million people around the globe died from tuberculosis in 2025, according to the World Health Organization. The disease is caused by mycobacteria that are difficult to combat with antibiotics. Multidrug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis that are impervious to many of the most effective tuberculosis antibiotics are particularly problematic, creating an urgent need for new drugs.

items.title: How a brainless single-celled slime mold solves problems using the laws of physics
items.blurb: If you watched the single-celled slime mold Physarum polycephalum for a short while, you could be forgiven for thinking that it had some form of intelligence. It can solve mazes, find the shortest routes between food sources and learn from experience. Yet it has no brain or nervous system. So how does it pull that off without a mind to guide it?

If AI also became capable of moral agency, it might one day have a claim to political voice.

items.title: Removing background noise brings cellular properties into focus
items.blurb: When light interacts with a material, a small part of it gets scattered with a different energy. This change can reveal information about the molecules within the material based on their unique molecular fingerprints. This phenomenon, which earned physicist C. V. Raman the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, forms the basis of Raman spectroscopy, a widely used technique for studying the chemical composition of materials.

By targeting multiple strains of the bacteria, this rapid detection approach has the potential to enable targeted therapy and reduce the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics among critically ill patients.

items.title: Amber fossils reveal how grasshoppers may have walked on water 100 million years ago
items.blurb: Walking on water represents one of the most striking modes of locomotion in the natural world and plays a crucial role in animals' colonization of ecological niches at the water surface. However, insects specialized for this locomotion (obligate surface dwellers) belong to only two groups: the living Gerromorpha (Hemiptera) and extinct Chresmodidae (stem group of Polyneoptera). Elucidating how extinct insects moved on the water surface has proven highly challenging, and the adaptive evolution of different insect lineages to ecological niches at the water surface remains poorly understood.

items.title: New measurements suggest surrounding liquids control water layer formation on submerged ice
items.blurb: The behavior of ice exposed to a vacuum or vapor has been studied extensively, but ice submerged in a liquid is more difficult to study. Temperature changes cause the ice to dissolve or grow, resulting in fluctuating interfaces.

items.title: Most precise measurement of coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering to date tightens limits on new forces
items.blurb: Neutrinos are tiny elementary particles with little mass and no electric charge. While most neutrinos pass through matter without interacting, a neutrino can occasionally scatter off an atomic nucleus, transferring a little energy to it and causing it to move.

The study, conducted in Podocarpus National Park in southern Ecuador, found that mid-elevation forests harbor the greatest diversity of these microorganisms, while their richness decreases at higher elevations and their community composition differs.

items.title: How utilities, communities can help build resilience for vulnerable families during power outages
items.blurb: For low-income households, extended power outages can create devastating losses of food and money, as well as feelings of comfort and security within their homes, according to research led by the University of Michigan.

items.title: Board diversity and digital readiness linked to corporate adaptability during pandemic
items.blurb: Think "pandemic" and the word "pivot" is not far behind. What happened to organizational communications during COVID-19, though, was an unprecedented sea change. For businesses trying to stay connected to investors like pension and mutual funds, in-person roadshows, brokerage-hosted conferences and "analyst day" meetings were adapted into virtual versions filtered through the safety of personal digital devices as everyone hunkered down at home.

items.title: Ant rivalry temporarily protects native ants until one invader takes over
items.blurb: When an invasive species enters a natural habitat, it can start competing for resources with native species and threaten their survival. If more than one invasive species occupies the same habitat, the interactions between them can further contribute to the damage and disruption that ensues.

Despite encouraging progress over the past decade, researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.

items.title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
items.blurb: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Not everything that sounds plausible works: Testing ideas to win support for carbon pricing
items.blurb: What makes people support a carbon price? To find out, 108 researchers, led by a research team at the University of Innsbruck, Austria, tested 55 different ideas at the same time, from information campaigns to reflection tasks. On average, there was a small but statistically significant positive effect. Individually, the effect was detectable for only 11 of the 55 ideas. One of the strongest effects came from writing a letter to a fictional person of a future generation. The results were recently published in the journal Nature Human Behaviour.

items.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
items.blurb: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

items.title: AI is forcing researchers to confront the possibility of artificial minds

items.title: New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010
items.blurb: The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025. The main drivers are sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law.

items.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
items.blurb: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

items.title: Queensland keeps learning disaster lessons. So why do we keep forgetting them?
items.blurb: After an early start to Queensland's storm season, with severe storms and flooding already affecting communities across the state, attention is once again turning to disaster preparedness and response.

items.title: A star's 'obliquity' likely has little impact on a given planet's habitability
items.blurb: A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumstellar disk that surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar-type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star's initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

items.title: What draws data centers to a community?
items.blurb: As Oklahoma communities weigh new data center development, research co-authored by a University of Oklahoma architecture professor offers insight into what draws major technology companies to locations—and why those choices matter locally.

items.title: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Niño fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic
items.blurb: The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends on Nov. 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Niño. Below-normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii.

items.title: Ultrathin 'rainbow' sails could power spacecraft and shade the Earth
items.blurb: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind "solar sailing," which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed feasible.

items.title: How alfalfa forms root nodules without rhizobia
items.blurb: A research team led by professor Feng Jian at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology (IGDB) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a cytokinin–NODULE INCEPTION (NIN) regulatory module associated with spontaneous root nodule formation in alfalfa (Medicago sativa).

items.title: New chemical route delivers first synthesis of plant compound with cough-suppressing potential
items.blurb: Neotuberostemonine, a complex plant-derived alkaloid with promising antitussive activity, has remained a challenging target for chemical synthesis for nearly 30 years. Researchers have now achieved its first total synthesis, alongside the synthesis of neostenine and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. The findings also reveal how the nearly planar geometry of nitrogen atoms contributes to the oxidative instability of these alkaloids, offering new insights and synthetic strategies for natural-product chemistry and future drug discovery.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
items.blurb: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.

items.title: Quantum ingenuity can sidestep limits of conventional chips—while using commercially accessible components
items.blurb: For decades, computers have steadily grown faster and more powerful. Avik Dutt, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Maryland, envisions another dramatic leap forward—one propelled by the quantum properties of light.

items.title: Laser light reveals where electrons accumulate in atomically thin semiconductor stacks
items.blurb: Stacking semiconductors—the chips that power phones, computers and so much more—enables quicker signal movement with less energy, but how does the process actually work? Turns out shining a literal light on the semiconducting materials can help elucidate how the electrons move in the stack, according to a multi-institutional team in Japan. The approach could help inform the development of more efficient, low-power electronics, the researchers said.

items.title: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea
items.blurb: Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. More than 20 years ago, researchers observed an unfamiliar salp in the deep waters of Monterey Bay. Using specimens and data collected by MBARI's advanced underwater robots, Larry Madin, deputy director emeritus at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and an MBARI adjunct, recently published a detailed description of the glass salp (Vitreosalpa gemini) in the journal Marine Biodiversity. This striking species is the first salp known to live exclusively in the deep sea.

items.title: Myanmar earthquake reveals how fault history could help anticipate future slip
items.blurb: Earthquakes are full of unknowns—scientists can't accurately predict exactly when or where the next big earthquake will strike. But some characteristics of 'the next big one' can be anticipated from what we know about a fault before it breaks, thanks to supercomputer simulations combined with an ever-increasing wealth of observational data.

items.title: New workflow advances programmable chromosome editing in plants
items.blurb: A study published in Nature Protocols on Nov. 17 presents a detailed experimental workflow for programmable chromosome manipulation in plants. The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

items.title: Later-born generations have better memory and lose it more slowly
items.blurb: Nature Medicine, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04758-z Dementia risk at any age has been falling for decades. An analysis of ~219,000 people followed for up to 30 years shows that newer generations start old age with a larger cognitive capacity that declines more slowly than that of previous generations, and this combined advantage is large enough to account for the fall in dementia incidence.

items.title: High dietary sucrose reveals distinct roles for the BBSome subunits BBS1 and BBS9 in Drosophila development
items.blurb: Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes occur in Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and BBSome proteins regulate insulin receptor abundance at the cell surface in mammals. We asked how loss of two structurally related BBSome subunits, BBS1 and BBS9, affects development on a high-sucrose diet in Drosophila melanogaster. Sequence comparisons identified the seven-bladed beta-propeller and gamme-adaptin ear domains of human BBS1 and BBS9 in their respective fly orthologues. High sucrose (1 M) delayed pupariation in both single mutants, with the longest delay in flies lacking both subunits. The double mutant already showed a delay on standard sucrose (0.15 M). On high sucrose, its first pupae were recorded at 216 h after egg laying, whereas the last control and single-mutant pupae had formed by 168 h. Loss of BBS1 also reduced pupal volume and adult wing area on high sucrose. Both measurements remained close to control values in BBS9 mutants. These findings suggest overlapping contributions of BBS1 and BBS9 to developmental timing and a greater requirement for BBS1 to sustain growth under high dietary sucrose.

items.title: Inhibition of Bacteriophage Infection by Natural and Synthetic DNA-binding Compounds
items.blurb: The arms race between bacteria and phages involves a wide range of immune and anti-immune systems on both sides. One of the long-known mechanisms of antiphage defense involves DNA intercalators such as daunorubicin and its analogues. Daunorubicin was also shown to inhibit bacterial growth as well as eukaryotic cell division, underlying its use in chemotherapy. Other DNA intercalators and minor groove binding dyes are widely used for nucleic acids staining, but have not been studied for their effects on viral infection. Here, we systematically investigate the effects of known intercalator and DNA-binding agents, including daunorubicin and Hoechst derivatives, on phage infection in Escherichia coli. Using a diverse panel of phages with various replication mechanisms we identify phylogenetic groups sensitive to DNA-binding dyes and determined which stage of the viral life cycle was inhibited. Our data suggest that the active antiviral compounds block early steps of infection without cells killing, arguing against an abortive infection mechanism and lethal membrane permeabilization suggested recently. Together, our results expand the list of small molecules that affect phage infection and reveal DNA binders that inhibit viral DNA entry and/or replication without affecting cell physiology.

items.title: PAannotate: Software for Exploring Pseudomonas aeruginosa Gene-Expression Associations from Transcriptomic Data
items.blurb: With the proliferation of transcriptomic data for Pseudomonas aeruginosa there is a need for software programs able to efficiently analyze both individual transcriptomes as well as large, publicly available compendiums of arrays. PAannotate is an R package and native macOS application capable of analyzing the Whiteley Lab database of 5,821 transcriptomes from 470 BioProjects. In the application, researchers can use recorded metadata such as strain, medium or treatment to select experiments or genes associated with particular expression patterns. Alternatively, selecting one gene of interest, a user can find other, coordinately regulated genes that move together across many environments, mutants, and treatments. PAannotate also allows users to select groups of genes and to use Gene Ontology and KEGG annotations and enrichment analysis to see whether those genes are associated with particular biological functions more often than expected by chance, determine whether a particular perturbation produces a reproducible response across studies, or find public experiments resembling your own experiment. Researchers can build and customize heatmaps and association networks. In one project, we have examined the P. aeruginosa transcriptomic associations with the genes encoding the Pf prophage present in P. aeruginosa strain PAO1. We found a strong negative correlation between PA0724, a Pf4 gene, and ccmG, a bacterial gene involved in energy metabolism. We identified that much of this relationship was reflected by a difference in whether the bacteria were grown with acetate or glycerol as their carbon source. This finding illustrates how PAannotate helps researchers investigate P. aeruginosa gene correlations.

items.title: Salmonella MgtC promotes polymyxin B resistance and systemic infection by activating LpxO-mediated lipid A hydroxylation
items.blurb: The intracellular pathogen Salmonella Typhimurium modifies the lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide through various lipid A-modifying enzymes, thereby acquiring resistance to host cationic antimicrobial peptides during infection. While regulation of these enzymes at the transcription level has been extensively studied, however, regulation at the activity level remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the Salmonella virulence factor MgtC interacts with LpxO, an enzyme that hydroxylates the 3'-myristoyl chain of hexa-acylated lipid A, identified through bacterial two-hybrid screening for potential MgtC interaction partners. MgtC binding to LpxO promotes lipid A hydroxylation in a concentration-dependent manner, and the Leu287 residue in the C-terminal helix of LpxO is required for this interaction. Substitution of Leu287 with Ala reduces MgtC binding without affecting intrinsic hydroxylase activity, consequently impairing MgtC-enhanced lipid A hydroxylation. This substitution decreases resistance to both the antimicrobial peptide polymyxin B and human serum, and attenuates virulence in a mouse infection model. These findings suggest that Salmonella exploits MgtC to promote LpxO hydroxylation activity, thereby enhancing survival inside the host.

items.title: SimpleP2G: Importance of Image Encoders for Gene Expression Prediction from Pathology Images
items.blurb: Pathology-image-to-gene-expression (P2G) studies often change the prediction head, image encoder, and spatial context together, making performance differences difficult to attribute. We examine these factors through paired image-input controls and explicit input regimes. Our main comparison covers five HEST-1K datasets, two 200-gene panels, and three selected held-out slides per dataset, using validation-selected checkpoints. Across all five datasets, replacing conventional image inputs with Virchow2 improves mean PCC-200 in 39 of 40 method--dataset--panel comparisons, while one comparison decreases. We introduce SimpleP2G, a direct gene-query decoder over frozen embeddings, and SimpleP2G-cross, which adds spatially positioned neighboring embeddings. With shared Virchow2 features, SimpleP2G has the highest single-patch mean PCC-200 on all five datasets under both panels; the cross-patch variant leads on four of five datasets under each panel. Decoder and context ablations show that greater depth and broader context do not consistently improve prediction. Together, these results suggest improving image representations before adding prediction-head complexity: a direct decoder over frozen pathology embeddings already provides a strong baseline. We hope our reimplemented image-encoder-upgraded baselines and SimpleP2G models serve as transparent, reproducible, and strong controls for future P2G research.

items.title: Distinct chaperones coordinate the type III secretion system assembly and effector secretion in Vibrio parahaemolyticus
items.blurb: Many Gram-negative bacterial pathogens rely on the type III secretion system (T3SS) to deliver virulence factors or effectors into host cells. In Vibrio parahaemolyticus, the leading cause of seafood-borne gastroenteritis, one of the two T3SSs, the T3SS2, is essential for intestinal colonization and infection in the human body. While many T3SS2 effectors have been extensively characterized, the chaperones that guide their biogenesis and coordinate assembly of the T3SS machinery remain poorly understood. Here, combining comparative transcriptomic and proteomic approaches with functional analyses, we reveal that four T3SS2 chaperones exert non-overlapping control over distinct clients for pathogenesis. We further show that these chaperones form a hierarchical, multi-layered checkpoint system that ensures the temporal order of secretion, coordinating injectisome assembly, pore formation, and effector deployment. Our findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding the regulation of T3SS2, demonstrating that discrete non-redundant chaperone-mediated assembly is conserved across diverse Gram-negative pathogens.

items.title: A microbiota-dependent fitness locus promotes intraspecies competition and cell envelope resilience in gut bacterium Phocaeicola vulgatus
items.blurb: A central question in gut microbial ecology is how dominant bacterial species establish and occupy their niches amid inter- and intraspecies competition. Phocaeicola vulgatus (Pvu) is a Gram-negative anaerobe and prevalent member of the human gut microbiome that can integrate into established gut communities without antibiotic pretreatment, yet mechanisms underlying this competitive success remain poorly understood. Using in vivo transposon insertion sequencing, we identified a three-gene locus that promotes Pvu intraspecies fitness in the presence of a complex microbiota but is dispensable in germ-free hosts. The locus encodes a predicted HU/IHF superfamily histone-like DNA-binding protein (DifH), a hypothetical lipid-binding protein (DifS), and a FadL-like outer-membrane transporter (DifT). In vitro genetic and transcriptomic analyses implicated these genes in cell envelope resilience. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing revealed that DifH binds a specific repetitive DNA motif at its own locus and a limited set of additional loci involved in metabolism, envelope biogenesis, and cellular defense. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized fitness locus that promotes cell envelope resilience, enables intraspecies competition, and supports Pvu persistence within complex gut microbial communities. More broadly, these results uncover mechanisms by which this dominant gut commensal secures its niche and suggests avenues to therapeutically modulate gut microbiota composition.

items.title: Phage integrons are vaults of privatized counterdefense genes
items.blurb: Integrons facilitate the adaptation of microbes by capturing beneficial gene cassettes, including antiphage defense systems, but their role in phage adaptation remains unclear. Here, we identify reversed integron cassette organization in phages, with 96% of reverse-oriented cassettes lacking detectable homologs in surveyed bacterial and plasmid integrons. Phage cassettes are enriched in counterdefenses, including viral sponge-like proteins. Despite these differences, representative phage and bacterial integron integrases recombine cassette attachment sites from either source; however, exchange between oppositely organized phage and bacterial integron arrays misorients incoming gene cassettes relative to the recipient integron's promoter, posing an expression barrier. These findings establish integrons as a shared engine of the phage-host arms race, capturing defenses in bacteria and counterdefenses in phages, while cassette orientation buffers exchange between the two adaptive repertoires.

items.title: Local protein supply chain keeps nerve cells' mitochondria in check
items.blurb: Some tracers used in hospital scans to check what is happening inside a patient's body are so short-lived they must be made on demand on site or rushed in by courier. A new study led by Angelika Harbauer's group at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence shows that nerve cells use similar strategies to deliver a protein that checks for damage in their mitochondria, the tiny structures that supply energy, balance calcium levels and perform other vital tasks.

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.blurb: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

items.title: Sex in Britain has changed significantly, especially among young people
items.blurb: The sex lives of people in Britain have shifted markedly since 1990, and their sexual and reproductive health needs are substantial and varied, according to the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4). The first five papers from the survey—one of the largest studies of sexual behavior in the world—are published in The Lancet.

items.title: Microplastics in nearly 8 in 10 fish sampled off Oman's Sohar coast
items.blurb: Researchers at Sultan Qaboos University detected microplastics in the gills or digestive tracts of 95 of 120 fish sampled off Sohar in the Sea of Oman. Published in Scientific Reports, the study provides a baseline for tracking microplastic pollution in fish along this stretch of Oman's coast.

items.title: Blind sample test reveals how BepiColombo could decode Mercury's mineral makeup
items.blurb: An international team of researchers, including scientists from Planetary Science Institute (PSI), has demonstrated that instruments aboard the BepiColombo spacecraft can operate together to identify the minerals that make up Mercury's surface, addressing a longstanding challenge in planetary science. The findings, published in Planetary and Space Science, come as the joint European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission entered orbit around Mercury this week.

items.title: Carbon-rich soil near old oaks does not attract more earthworms, study finds
items.blurb: Solitary oaks in traditional Romanian wood pastures create islands of carbon-rich soil around their trunks. However, a research team led by the Universities of Göttingen and Hildesheim found this does not mean more earthworms. In traditional wood pastures in Romania, the topsoil near the trunk held about a third more organic carbon and a quarter more nitrogen than the open grassland, yet earthworm numbers were no higher. As such trees decline across Europe, it is important to understand what they contribute to the soil. The results were published in the journal Agroforestry Systems.

items.title: Self-assembling nanocarriers show promise for delivering CRISPR to tumors and slowing growth
items.blurb: A self-assembling supramolecular nanocarrier protects Cas9 RNPs from degradation, enhances systemic delivery and preferential tumor accumulation, and enables pH-responsive intracellular release. Developed by researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, this platform achieved a 37.2% indel frequency at the luciferase target locus in HeLa-Luc tumor tissue in mice, compared with 1.5% with free RNPs, and suppressed tumor growth in separate mouse models. These findings support the further development of systemic CRISPR-based cancer therapies.

items.title: Named 'Maria,' a new species of amphibian pays tribute to the world's most popular name
items.blurb: Maria, the most popular female name in Brazil and around the world, was chosen for a new species of caecilian, a type of amphibian commonly known as a "blind snake," found in this South American country. The researchers chose the name Siphonops maria to raise awareness of this little-known animal, even among researchers in the field.

items.title: The enjoy-able effect: Why fun makes us feel more skilled than we are
items.blurb: Picture a hobby, a game or an activity you love. Maybe it's cooking or Wordle or playing pickup basketball. For a long time, I have loved playing video games. Now ask yourself: How good are you at it?

items.title: NASA Hubble's new view of NGC 4394 raises the bar
items.blurb: A brilliant galaxy with a distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image. The galaxy, called NGC 4394, is in the constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice's Hair). At about 55 million light-years away, NGC 4394 is considered relatively nearby for a galaxy. It's one of more than 1,000 galaxies that make up the Virgo Cluster, which is the galaxy cluster closest to us.

items.title: Quantum blueprint maps a practical path to testing unusual entanglement
items.blurb: Adrian Del Maestro knows how to engineer a quantum fingerprint. Rick Mukherjee has a gift for tuning atoms. Their combined expertise has taken a theory sketched out on paper and created a pathway for real experiments. The results, published in the journal Physical Review Letters, move a law-defying "mathematical oddity" ever so slightly up the technology readiness scale

items.blurb: With the holidays approaching and the semester winding down, to-do lists are growing. Between shopping for gifts, planning gatherings, studying for finals and finishing projects, there's plenty to accomplish before the end of the year.

items.title: Flowers in Renaissance sculpture may reveal political ambitions of Florence's ruler
items.blurb: A new study suggests that the flowers adorning Benvenuto Cellini's sculpture Narcissus are more than decoration: they connect the development of botanical science with competition among Renaissance artists and the ambition of Florence's ruler to consolidate his status.

items.title: Why mega-constellations have a hidden space junk blind spot
items.blurb: We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected 1 million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways.

items.title: A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster
items.blurb: Why are some groups of molecules remarkably stable while others readily break apart? Researchers at Bar-Ilan University have discovered a surprising explanation for why clusters containing exactly six molecules of glycine, the simplest amino acid, are exceptionally stable—making six a "magic number." Moreover, they have uncovered the reason for this increased stability. The secret lies in a transformation that takes place when the molecules come together: they change their structure and become zwitterions, allowing them to form stronger bonds with one another.

items.title: Mindfulness training may bring out the worst in some employees
items.blurb: Contrary to popular belief, mindfulness training in the workplace can make some employees angrier and more likely to treat coworkers with disrespect.

items.title: Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations
items.blurb: Tropical cyclones frequently undergo rapid, complex structural changes within their inner cores, such as eyewall replacement and wind-field expansion, that strongly influence typhoon intensity and coastal hazards. However, capturing these multilayered transformations continuously from the ocean surface to the upper cloud tops remains a major observational challenge.

items.title: DNA at nuclear edges forms protective UV shield in developing roundworm embryos
items.blurb: Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is arranged into neighborhoods, some of which are tightly packed and mostly inactive. This so-called heterochromatin typically associates with the nuclear lamina, a meshwork lining the inside of the nuclear envelope. This arrangement helps organize the genome and regulate gene activity. But how and when it forms during embryonic development has remained unclear.

items.title: An intragastric murine model that recapitulates natural infection with invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella for preclinical evaluation of vaccine immunogenicity and protection.
items.blurb: Invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella disease is a major global health concern, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where young children and immunocompromised individuals are particularly vulnerable. Preclinical models that reproduce the natural course of invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella infection without antibiotic-mediated disruption of the intestinal microbiota are essential for vaccine development. Here, an antibiotic-free murine model is described based on intragastric infection of susceptible C57BL/6 mice with the ST313 clinical isolate Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium D23580. Over seven days, infection progressed from intestinal colonization to extraintestinal dissemination, accompanied by increasing histopathological damage and activation of local and systemic inflammatory responses. The ability of the infection model to evaluate vaccine-induced immunity and protection was assessed by immunizing mice with a formalin-inactivated D23580 strain. Vaccination elicited Salmonella-specific serum IgG and reduced clinical severity, with vaccinated mice showing significantly lower bacterial loads in blood, liver and colon compared with control mice after intragastric challenge. By combining the enteric route, which mimics the natural route of human infection, with an intact intestinal microbiota, this model reproduces key features of progressive invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella disease and provides a tool for investigating host-pathogen interactions and evaluating vaccine-induced immunity and protection.

items.title: ModFormer: A unified structure-aware model of transcriptome-wide A-to-I RNA editing
items.blurb: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing can recode transcripts without permanently altering the genome. ADAR-catalyzed editing depends on both local sequence and RNA secondary structure, making it difficult to anticipate which sites will be edited or how mutations will change their activity. Moving from observing endogenous A-to-I editing to using it as a programmable molecular tool requires predicting how editing responds to sequence changes. Here, we present ModFormer, a model that integrates RNA sequence representations with predicted secondary structure to predict ADAR-mediated editing. Trained on human data, ModFormer predicts editing sites and rates across substrates and species unseen during training, recovers established sequence and pairing preferences, and anticipates experimentally measured responses to RNA mutations. These predictions prioritize responsive sites in mutational screens and guide an autonomous AI agent toward candidate RNA designs. ModFormer provides a framework for predicting how sequence changes reshape RNA editing and can be adapted to new substrates with limited experimental data.

items.title: From hands to tools: evidence for evolutionary precursors of tool processing in macaque cortex.
items.blurb: In humans, hands are animate effectors and tools are visually dissimilar inanimate objects, yet the brain represents them in closely related cortical systems. Whether this coupling depends uniquely on human tool knowledge or reflects a conserved property of primate cortex is unknown. Using whole brain fMRI (0.22 cubic mm voxels) in macaques viewing images of hands, tools, and other objects, we found that inferotemporal cortex largely followed the animate/inanimate division, with only a few small hand-tool preferring sites. In contrast, parietal and prefrontal areas showed hand-tool representational similarities that were best matched by a neural-network model trained on fine-grained human hand-object interactions rather than by networks optimized for static object recognition or general action recognition. Volumetric functional ultrasound imaging (0.0023 cubic mm voxels) independently showed that tool responses were spatially aligned with human hand, but not monkey hand, responses in posterior parietal cortex. Macaque cortex thus represents tools in relation to the hand even without habitual tool use, consistent with an evolutionarily conserved action related scaffold that may be shaped by longterm visual exposure to human hand tool interactions.

items.title: Use of orthogonal split inteins to direct surface expression of specific metabotropic glutamate receptor hererodimer pairs.
items.blurb: Metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) are class C G protein coupled receptors that function as obligate, covalently linked homo- and heterodimers in some combinations. The pharmacological responses of heterodimers to selective ligands are difficult to predict, and due to the tendency to homodimerize, heterodimers cannot be easily expressed in isolation. Here, we developed a split-intein-based approach to preferentially direct the plasma membrane expression of defined mGluR heterodimers, enabling their pharmacological characterization with minimal homodimer interference. Our strategy employs orthogonal split inteins flanking an endoplasmic reticulum retention/internalization sequence within the receptor C-terminal tail. Association of receptors carrying complementary intein modules promotes protein trans-splicing, removing the trafficking restriction and allowing receptor delivery to the cell surface. Following a systematic screening, the orthogonal Avi PRP8 and Mja KlbA inteins (designated C and F) were selected to generate complementary constructs. Co-expression of these constructs produced functional responses from multiple group II and III mGluR combinations, whereas individually expressed receptors generally lacked detectable signaling. Pharmacological characterization of mGlu2/4 using subtype-selective agonists supported the preferential expression of functional heterodimers over homodimers. Furthermore, glutamate dose-response profiles of most CF/FC receptor combinations closely resembled those obtained using the heterodimer-selective CODA-RET assay, supporting the ability of this approach to distinguish heterodimer-mediated signaling. Independent HiBiT-based surface-expression measurements confirmed partner-dependent membrane delivery while revealing receptor-specific limitations in retention efficiency, particularly for mGlu8-containing constructs. Together, these findings establish orthogonal split inteins as a tool for the selective functional and pharmacological characterization of mGluR heterodimers while minimizing interference from homodimer signaling.

items.title: PTMlink: a database resource for co-variation of glycosylation and phosphorylation in human tumors
items.blurb: Protein glycosylation and phosphorylation can regulate each other, but the two protein modifications are usually studied separately, and their modification-specific co-variation across tumor types remains poorly characterized. PTMlink is a database of site-resolved co-variation between glycosylation and phosphorylation in the matched glycoproteomes and phosphoproteomes of 1,211 tumor samples from cohorts of the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium, complemented by studies that perturbed glycosylation in human cells to examine its crosstalk with, and functional effects on, phosphorylation. Eligible glycosite- phosphosite pairs are scored within each tumor cohort by a covariate-adjusted partial rank correlation and combined across cohorts by meta-analysis, where specific glycoforms are scored in the same way and gene pairs are summarized. The strongest associations reproduce in held-out tumor types and show concordance in normal adjacent tissue, and the strongest pairs are enriched for known protein interactions and shared pathways; perturbation evidence recovers literature-documented relations that co-variation misses. Available through a website, an R package and a Model Context Protocol server, PTMlink is, to our knowledge, the first resource to provide a queryable score for site-specific relations between glycosylation and phosphorylation across tumor cohorts, with a framework that can extend to other protein modifications as matched measurements become available.

items.title: Cold atmospheric plasma for improved sustainability and fish welfare in recirculating aquaculture systems
items.blurb: Decontamination of water is mandatory for the cultivation of aquatic species in recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS). Avoiding economic and ecological losses while ensuring safe conditions is important for the future introduction of new technologies. Therefore, the implementation of cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) within RAS was examined for the first time. For the integration of this technology two equal RAS were set up, one using CAP, the other one ultraviolet light (UV) for water decontamination. Experiments with Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) were performed for three weeks to compare CAP with UV as reference. The CAP device was switched on intermittently for 8 hours daily (with intervals of 10 min on and 30 min off), while two UV lamps were turned on continuously throughout the entire time of 3 weeks, which required more energy. Fish development was tracked by fish weight and stress levels (cortisol measurements). Values for pH, conductivity, oxygen, temperature, microbial load, microbiome and ion composition were also monitored. Microbial loads for both setups were reduced by four orders of magnitude. The biodiversity of the microbiome of the two technologies was similar with a beta-diversity between 19 and 25. Deviations within each setup were low with the alpha-diversity ranging from 2.23-2.93 (CAP) and 2.42-2.79 (UV). The water monitoring revealed similar results for pH value, conductivity, oxygen and temperature. No differences for the cortisol measurements and also the fish weight were determined. The results demonstrate CAP as a competitive and more energy efficient alternative to UV benefiting fish welfare and development in a similar way. The equal development of fish and water parameters and low energy consumption compared to UV makes CAP an energy efficient tool, likewise enhancing fish welfare.

items.title: A cell-based screen identifies host-directed inhibitors and nutrient-conditional antimicrobials against intracellular S. flexneri dissemination
items.blurb: Multidrug-resistant S. flexneri is a World Health Organization priority pathogen for which no universally licensed vaccine is currently available. Most antimicrobial screening platforms involve planktonic bacteria replicating in nutrient-rich medium, a condition that does not reflect the intracellular niche in which S. flexneri replicates and spreads and systematically excludes compounds whose activity depends on the host environment. Here, we screened the 1,581 compounds of the National Cancer Institute Diversity Set VII for inhibitors of S. flexneri dissemination in human colonic HT-29 monolayers by high-content microscopy. By applying sequential counter-screens, we identified six hits falling into two mechanistically distinct classes. Four compounds restricted dissemination without detectable antibacterial activity or host toxicity at the concentrations used. NSC310113 and Thiosangivamycin (NSC105827) implicate host matrix metalloprotease activity in cell-to-cell spread and host CDK2 in epithelial cell invasion. Two additional compounds, NSC45641 and NSC367428, were antibacte-rial only under nutrient-limited conditions and would have been described as inactive by conventional screening. NSC45641 is an adenine analog imposing a purine limitation reversible by adenine supplementation. The uracil analog NSC367428, whose activity requires the bacterial uracil phosphoribosyltransferase Upp, is consistent with perturbation of pyrimidine metabolism in both minimal medium and in HT-29 cells. Together, these findings demonstrate that cell-based dissemination screening of the NCI Diversity Set VII identified two classes of inhibitors that would likely be missed by conventional nutrient-rich medium screening, highlighting nutrient-conditional antimicrobials as promising starting points for developing treatments against intracellular pathogens.

items.title: Assessment of dopaminergic neurotoxicity of CYP2E1-mediated trichloroethylene metabolites in C. elegans
items.blurb: Trichloroethylene (TCE) is an industrial solvent associated with Parkinson's Disease (PD). Studies have demonstrated that TCE undergoes extensive metabolism in humans, suggesting that TCE toxicity may be attributable to its metabolites. However, knowledge of how TCE metabolites contribute to neurotoxicity in PD remains limited. We exposed Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) to the TCE metabolites trichloroacetic acid (TCA) and trichloroethanol (TCEOH) to determine if exposure disrupts dopamine-dependent behaviors, such as movement and egg retention, and impairs dopamine neuron viability. TCA and TCEOH were selected because we have demonstrated that they are either detected or likely present in mouse brain after a human-relevant inhalation exposure to TCE. Wild-type, GFP-expressing, and an a-synuclein-expressing strain were exposed to 5 mM TCEOH, 10 mM TCA, or control doses. Dopaminergic neuronal viability and movement was assessed following 5 days of exposure and revealed a lack of pronounced neurodegeneration or deficits in movement following either exposure. However, TCEOH exposure for 2 days resulted in changes in egg retention, suggesting that it may disrupt dopaminergic or serotonergic neurotransmission. Although C. elegans-based assays can identify changes in PD-relevant outcomes, this study suggests that TCA and TCEOH in this exposure paradigm display limited morphological or behavioral toxicity in C. elegans, warranting further investigation of these metabolites in additional C. elegans and mammalian studies.

items.title: Evaluating WGS-based methods as an in silico replacement of phage typing for historical continuity and host association in Salmonella Typhimurium
items.blurb: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STm) poses a significant burden on public health worldwide. The Anderson phage typing scheme has historically supported surveillance, outbreak investigations and source attribution through associations between phage types and animal hosts. However, limitations inherent to the scheme have led to the gradual replacement of phage typing by whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-based methods. In this study, we applied statistical and machine learning approaches to 1,329 high-quality STm whole-genome sequences to compare phage typing with hierarchical clustering of core-genome multilocus sequence typing (HierCC) and the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) address. We observed low congruence (< 0.60) between phage typing and WGS-based approaches. Nevertheless, a random forest model using WGS-based subtypes as features was able to predict all phage types with high specificity ([≥] 0.94) and at least 80% recall for 10 of the 24 analysed phage types. These included phage types of human and veterinary epidemiological importance, including DT193, DT104, DT2, DT40, DT56, DT9, and DT99. We then assessed whether WGS-based subtyping methods could replace the host-association feature of phage typing. At higher distance thresholds ([≥] 100) WGS-based subtyping methods were more informative of animal host species and displayed stronger host-associations than phage types for 11 of the 12 animal hosts, with significantly stronger associations for ducks, finches, and pigs (all p < 0.05). Thus, despite low congruence between phage types and WGS-based subtypes, our random forest model accurately predicted several epidemiologically important phage types, including those important to public health and veterinary surveillance, supporting its potential as an in silico alternative for those phage types. Finally, our findings suggest HierCC and SNP address methods can capture the host-association information historically derived from phage typing.

items.title: The Dark Side of Light: Adolescent Light Exposure at Night Disrupts Hippocampal Clocks and Plasticity-Related Signaling in a Sex-Dependent Manner.
items.blurb: In today's society, adolescents are being increasingly exposed to artificial blue light at night from electronic devices, raising concerns about its effects on brain development and mental health. The hippocampus, and specifically the dentate gyrus (DG) regulates memory formation and itself operates as a subordinate circadian oscillator detecting changes in the light environment. However, whether light at night during adolescence can impair hippocampal clock and function remains unknown. To begin exploring this, we exposed adolescent mice to a light cycle disruption (LCD) paradigm consisting of 12hrs of light followed by 5hrs of darkness and 7hrs of blue-enriched light for 5 consecutive days per week, followed by a standard 12 hours of light and 12 hours of darkness (12L:12D) for 2 days, over a 4-week period. Control animals were maintained under standard 12L:12D. Female and male mice were then tested for novel object recognition (NOR) and novel object location (NOL), and brain tissues were collected for clock gene expression, neuroplasticity markers, and dendritic spine analyses. We found that male mice exposed to LCD spent less time exploring novel objects and locations, and more time with familiar ones, a pattern consistent with impaired recognition and spatial memory, while female mice showed preserved memory performance despite LCD exposure. LCD-exposed male mice showed altered hippocampal daily expression rhythms of Clock and CRY2 levels compared to male control and LCD-exposed females. In addition, we found that LCD-exposed males exhibited reduced p-CREB expression along with reduced Bdnf and dendrite spines numbers in the DG. Interestingly, returning LCD-exposed males to standard 12L:12D conditions for 4 weeks were sufficient to reverse both the behavioral and molecular phenotypes. Together, these results suggest that chronic exposure to light at night during adolescence impairs memory in male mice, through alteration in hippocampal circadian clock regulation and plasticity-related mechanisms within the DG.

items.title: Rapamycin Mitigates Branched-Chain Amino Acid Accumulation in Maple Syrup Urine Disease Mice
items.blurb: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an inborn error of metabolism caused by mutations in the mitochondrial branched-chain -keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) complex, resulting in toxic accumulation of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) and their corresponding branched-chain keto acids (BCKAs). This leads to poorly understood clinical features in both brain and muscle. Due to a limited understanding of MSUD pathophysiology, there is a marked paucity of effective pharmacological interventions. Here, we discovered the mTOR inhibitor, rapamycin, improves disease and extends survival in MSUD mouse models. Rapamycin treatment attenuates neuroinflammation and reduces muscle pathology. To investigate the mechanism behind these effects, we studied the accumulation of BCAAs and BCKAs. Rapamycin decreased BCAA accumulation. Overall, our work identifies rapamycin as a potential therapy for MSUD. More broadly, it suggests dysregulated mTOR signaling may drive MSUD pathobiology and advances our understanding of the mechanisms influencing leucine toxicity.

items.title: ELLA-mix: Detecting Cell-to-Cell Heterogeneity in Subcellular RNALocalization
items.blurb: Subcellular RNA localization can differ between cells expressing the same gene, yet most analyses summarize transcript positions with a single gene-level pattern. We propose ELLA-mix, a finite mixture model for identifying cell subpopulations with distinct radial localization patterns from imaging-based spatial transcriptomics data. Transcript positions are normalized relative to the cell boundary and modeled using flexible spline densities within a count-conditioned nonhomogeneous Poisson process framework. Conditioning on each cell's transcript count separates differences in localization from differences in abundance. We estimate component densities and cell memberships using an expectation-maximization algorithm and select the number of patterns using the Bayesian information criterion, restricting consideration to models with stable cell assignments and sufficiently distinct components. Simulation studies evaluated the type I error and power of the test for nonuniform localization, as well as the accuracy of selecting the number of mixture components and estimating their radial distributions. ELLA-mix correctly selected the number of components in most simulated settings. In seqFISH+ mouse fibroblasts, ELLA-mix identified distinct cell subpopulations for genes previously assigned a single localization class; genes showing such variation were enriched for endoplasmic reticulum and extracellular matrix functions. In Xenium ovarian cancer tissue, more peripheral localization patterns were associated with higher proportions of proliferating cells, particularly in S phase. These results show how modeling cell-to-cell variation can reveal localization patterns and biological associations obscured by gene-level summaries.

items.title: The neural basis of unfamiliar face recognition in humans with fMRI frequency-tagging
items.blurb: Faces provide the most diagnostic information for identifying individuals in humans. Understanding the neural mechanisms involved in face identity recognition (FIR) is particularly important for unfamiliar faces, for which identity cannot rely on encoded multimodal semantic associations. Here, we investigated the neural basis of FIR using an original frequency-tagging fMRI approach providing objective, sensitive, and reliable measures of face recognition. Ten human participants were presented within a rapid 6 Hz stream of natural images of a single unfamiliar identity in two conditions: (1) with the same face image across low-level changes (size, luminance, contrast) only, or (2) with images varying in background, size, head orientation, gaze direction, etc. Every 9 s during a 243 s run, seven images of different unfamiliar identities were introduced in bursts. For each participant and each condition, we recorded runs with upright and inverted faces. Analyses were performed within face-selective regions (defined from a frequency-tagging localizer) and in the Fourier domain, where individual face discrimination responses were objectively identified and quantified at the identity-change frequency (0.111 Hz). We observed robust image-based individual face discrimination responses across both conditions in core face-selective ventral regions (LatMidFG and IOG). In contrast, responses in early visual cortex and the pSTS were negligible in our second condition, which required generalization across viewpoint variations. In addition, the LatMidFG showed a reliable inversion effect, confirming that the observed responses cannot be attributed solely to low-level image differences. Overall, these findings highlight the value of fMRI frequency-tagging for objectively characterizing the cortical network underlying unfamiliar FIR, providing evidence for high-level discrimination and generalization of unfamiliar face identity in the human ventral occipito-temporal face-selective network.

items.title: AVF creation in mice disrupts blood flow patterns to impact vasoreactivity
items.blurb: Maladaptive venous remodeling contributes to the high rate of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) maturation failure. Impaired vasoreactivity might impact this pathology. We created a murine AVF by anastomosing the external jugular vein to the carotid artery, establishing the AVF vein (AVF-V) and proximal (PA) and distal (DA) carotid artery. We hypothesized that endothelium-dependent vasorelaxation is impaired in the AVF-V vs. the contralateral vein (contra-V) of 5-month-old mice of both sexes 21-days post-surgery, reasoning that abrupt exposure to arterial pressure and disturbed hemodynamics promote endothelial dysfunction. Further, because magnetic resonance imaging revealed lower blood flow velocity and wall shear stress in PA vs. DA 21-days post-surgery, we hypothesized that endothelial function is compromised in PA. Whereas the thromboxane A2 receptor (TP) agonist U-46619 evoked sufficient vasocontraction in the contra-V from which subsequent vasorelaxation could be evaluated, AVF-V responsiveness was insufficient for this assessment, potentially reflecting >5-fold increases in collagen content and intima-media thickness. Consistent with our arterial hypothesis, endothelium-dependent vasorelaxation was impaired in the PA vs. DA and contralateral artery, whereas vascular smooth muscle function, cross-sectional area, collagen area, and intima-media thickness were similar among segments. Low shear stress impairs endothelial autophagy, which supports endothelial nitric oxide generation and vasodilation. Colocalized fluorescence of p-eNOSS1177 with CD31+ cells, and autophagy-related protein 3 with CD31+ cells, as well as nitric oxide bioavailability, were lower in PA vs. DA. These findings suggest that differential blood flow patterns in PA vs. DA following AVF creation may modulate endothelial autophagy, nitric oxide generation, and endothelium-dependent vasorelaxation.

items.title: Integrating hydrogen-exchange experiments with conformational ensembles
items.blurb: Protein conformational dynamics are central to biological function but remain difficult to characterise at scale. Amide hydrogen exchange (HX), measured by NMR or mass spectrometry, probes these dynamics but requires computational models for integration with structural ensembles. We benchmark models for calculating HX from ensembles using a large literature-derived dataset spanning folded and intrinsically disordered proteins. We then develop a model that identifies exchange-competent amides from local structural descriptors while accounting for electrostatic effects. The model predicts protection across a broad dynamic range in ensembles generated by molecular dynamics and generative AI. HX-guided ensemble reweighting improves agreement with independent NMR, SAXS, and folding-stability measurements. Millisecond HX distinguishes and refines alternative ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins, while reweighting of structured proteins reveals folding intermediates and low-population excited states. These results establish HX as a quantitative restraint for ensemble reweighting and provide a scalable framework for benchmarking simulations and generative protein models.

items.title: From Growth Inhibition to Fluctuations: Testing an Ising Model of Bacterial Responses to Antibiotics
items.blurb: Complex networks of biochemical reactions have been proposed to exhibit emergent cooperativity that can be described by an effective Ising model, with a small number of parameters encoding collective interactions. Here this mapping is experimentally tested using the response of three bacterial species to a range of antibiotics acting on different cellular targets. The Ising description is compared to the conventional Hill model, examining both the mean growth-rate response and, importantly, its population growth-rate heterogeneity (PGRH). While both models describe the mean growth-rate dependence on antibiotic concentration comparably well, we find that the Ising model provides a markedly better description of PGRH, offering an additional and more stringent test of the collective description. The fitted Ising interaction strength is systematically related to the Hill exponent and increases with the functional distance of the antibiotic target from the protein-production machinery. These results provide experimental support for describing complex biochemical reaction networks through effective cooperative Ising interactions, and suggest that the collective response of bacterial growth to antibiotics reflects the organization of the underlying metabolic network.

items.title: Unipept in 2026: A Unified Web Platform for Comparative Metaproteomics Analysis
items.blurb: Metaproteomics studies the collective proteome of microbial communities to characterize their taxonomic composition and functional activity. Unipept has long supported such analyses, but organizing samples into projects, building targeted reference databases, and comparing samples across a study were only possible in a standalone desktop application. Here we present a major update that moves these workflows into the web application, so a complete multi-sample study can be assembled, analyzed, and shared without local installation. Samples can be compared both taxonomically and functionally, the latter by mapping enzymes onto metabolic pathways with the integrated PathwayPilot. The analyses also became more informative. The Peptonizer2000, now accelerated by the new NORI inference engine, adds confidence scores to taxonomic and functional results, and an optional filter removes common contaminants before analysis. The Unipept API itself was also reworked, with an optimized index and flexible memory loading that roughly doubled query throughput and lowered the memory needed for deployment. We demonstrate these capabilities on six datasets of a defined microbial community.

items.title: APEs: Agentic Prediction of Epitopes to Guide Antibody-Antigen Structure Prediction
items.blurb: Antibody-antigen complex prediction remains difficult because the surface recognized by a specific antibody is often uncertain, and model confidence may not distinguish alternative poses. We developed APEs (Agentic Prediction of Epitopes for Structure Prediction), an agentic system that retrieves public evidence, interprets predicted antibody and antigen structures, and produces ranked residue-level epitope hypotheses. For retrospective evaluation, web retrieval was restricted to sources released before each CASP target entry date. Across eight CASP16 and six released CASP17 targets, the top-ranked patch reached residue precision of at least 0.5 for nine of 14 targets. We then used the predicted epitopes to steer additional Protenix-v1 sampling and to compare steered finalists with the highest ipSAE unsteered model. The retrospective best selection across three independent router calls increased mean DockQ from 0.306 to 0.375; DockQ increased from 0.089 to 0.679 for H2321 and from 0.005 to 0.379 for H2346. These results show that publicly available evidence specific to the target antibody-antigen complex can serve as an inference-time signal for epitope localization, guided complex sampling, and model selection. We also release predictions for CASP17 targets whose experimental structures had not been released when the predictions were finalized, providing a prospective test of APEs (https://github.com/CSSB-SNU/ape).

items.title: In silico pipeline for identification of targets of plastic-derived chemicals
items.blurb: Plastic pollution is a growing global health concern, yet the specific human protein targets mediating the toxic effects of plastic-derived chemicals (PDCs) remain largely unknown. Here, we present an integrative in silico pipeline that combines transcriptomic data with structural bioinformatics to identify putative human plastic-derived targets. Through comparative analysis with their canonical ligands, we identified 27 potential targets showing global binding energies comparable to endogenous ligands (-5.26 vs -5.60 kcal/mol), and six cases in which plastic-derived compounds performed better. Chemical similarity analysis revealed very low structural resemblance between PDCs and canonical ligands, indicating that PDCs do not act as structural mimetics but instead exploit different interactions within the same binding cavities. In a proof-of-concept case, we showed that Deoxyribonuclease I (DNase I) binds BP2 with higher affinity than its canonical ligand PO-3 (median -5.85 vs -2.55 kcal/mol). It also forms hydrogen bonds with Asn192 and {pi}-stacking interactions with the catalytic histidine His274, a pattern conserved in bovine DNase I. Experimental validation confirmed that BP2 at 10- M inhibits DNA hydrolysis by 21.5% in bovine DNase I (p-value < 0.01) and 23.2% in recombinant human DNase I (p-value < 0.001). Our work establishes a robust, transferable computational framework for identifying protein targets of environmental contaminants and reveals that PDCs engage their targets through novel non-mimetic binding modes, with structural patterns that can be conserved across species. These findings may have significant implications for the safety assessment of plastic additives.

items.title: Fast draft assemblies using locally consistent parsing
items.blurb: Recent improvements in long-read sequencing accuracy, particularly the introduction of PacBio HiFi reads, have created new opportunities for more efficient sequence representations in genome assembly. In particular, variations of de Bruijn graphs (dBG), such as sparse dBG and minimizer-space dBG, provide efficient representations of sequences and have enabled genome assemblers to leverage the high accuracy of long-read data while maintaining low memory usage and fast analysis times. Locally consistent parsing (LCP) is another technique for compact sequence representation that partitions a string into nearly uniform, highly distinctive substrings in a consistent manner. In this work, we combine ideas from minimizer-space assembly and LCP to achieve a significant speedup in HiFi long-read assembly. Specifically, we define a locally consistent de Bruijn Graph (lcDBG), in which string partitions serve as the graph's building blocks. We introduce Gallifrey, a rapid PacBio HiFi assembler that outperforms the fastest existing tool, rust-mdbg, by >6x in runtime while requiring 2x less memory, assembling a human genome in under one minute on a standard laptop, while generating assemblies with comparable contiguity. Code for Gallifrey is freely available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/gallifrey.

items.title: Biomedical Text Embeddings Weakly Capture Chromatin Accessibility Similarity: A Large-Scale Measurement Study
items.blurb: Text metadata provides the most readily available description of public chromatin accessibility data, but it remains unclear how well it reflects similarity between the underlying chromatin profiles. We systematically compared pairwise cosine similarity matrices derived from 12 embedding types across 32,245 human assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC-seq) experiments obtained from ChIP-Atlas. The embeddings were two chromatin representations (Atacformer and regulatory potential, RP), three biomedical language models and one general-domain model applied to full metadata and to cell-type names alone, term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF), and a random baseline. We measured agreement using Spearman rank correlation, Mantel permutation tests, and top-k neighborhood overlap in the similarity matrices. Across the full dataset, text-derived similarities correlated with Atacformer similarities at {rho}=0.20 to 0.30. This text-Atacformer agreement was largely driven by experiments with relatively few called peaks, which were enriched for promoter regions (median 69 to 75% within 1 kb of a transcription start site for experiments with 100 to 10,000 peaks), resulting in similar chromatin representations regardless of cell type. Among the 17,232 experiments with at least 5,000 peaks, the text-Atacformer correlations dropped substantially ({rho}=0.011 to 0.016), with less than 0.1% of top-5 neighbors shared. Atacformer itself barely tracked cell type in this subset, with only 1.3% of an experiment's top-5 neighbors sharing its cell-type label (0.8% expected by chance). In contrast, text-RP agreement was weak but persisted ({rho}=0.06 to 0.10; 28 to 35% of top-5 neighbors shared), suggesting that both capture coarse cell-type identity. Most of the text-derived similarity signal in the full dataset came from sample titles, which mainly identify the submission and sequencing platform. Notably, TF-IDF matched or exceeded the language models in every correlation comparison. These findings indicate that text metadata is at best a coarse proxy for chromatin accessibility similarity, and highlight the importance of controlling for peak count when comparing chromatin representations across public repositories.

items.title: Benchmarking sample mispairing detection tools in complex cancer datasets
items.blurb: Sample mispairs are common and potentially costly mistakes, and therefore checking for sample mispairing is a crucial quality-control step in multimodal genomic studies. This study presents an independent benchmark of sample mispairing detection tools in multimodal transcriptomic cancer datasets. In pseudobulk experiments with known sample pairings, four tools achieved near-perfect F1 scores across datasets. In real-data experiments, three tools performed particularly well, and sample mispairs were identified in three of five datasets. Finally, a high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma dataset is reconstructed: resolving mispairs between two bulk RNA-sequencing modalities, resolving mispairs between pooled single-cell and bulk RNA-seq data, and reestablishing the connection between the transcriptomic data and patient metadata using genetic ancestry inference.

items.title: BioSensor-X: A Coverage-Aware Evidence-Integration and Benchmarking Framework for Transcription-Factor Prioritization in Microbial Biosensor Engineering
items.blurb: Transcription-factor (TF) prioritization in microbial biosensor engineering requires integration of heterogeneous molecular and regulatory evidence, yet benchmark-associated performance may be influenced by candidate coverage, annotation density, and information-flow structure. BioSensor-X was developed as a leakage-controlled, coverage-aware framework for evaluating heterogeneous transcriptomic and regulatory evidence for Escherichia coli TF prioritization. Six transcriptomic datasets were processed, of which three contributed candidate instances, yielding 360 candidate contexts representing 60 TFs. The framework integrated transcriptional responsiveness, regulatory specificity, regulon size as an annotation-density proxy, and curated regulatory evidence using discovery-only standardization, prespecified equal weighting, and TF-level maximum aggregation. Performance was evaluated using mutually exclusive TF-level DEVELOPMENT and LOCKED TEST partitions with family-aware stratification, while candidate coverage was assessed separately from conditional ranking performance. Of 12 LOCKED TEST TFs, five were represented in the discovery candidate universe, corresponding to 41.7% coverage. The primary BioSensor-X score achieved a conditional AUROC of 0.5782 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.3308-0.8109), with 1/5 TFs recovered in the Top-10 and 2/5 in the Top-20. The regulon-size/annotation-density component achieved an AUROC of 0.7945 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.6655-0.9055). The integrated framework retained a measurable benchmark-associated ranking signal, while the results also indicated that annotation structure contributed substantially to benchmark discrimination. These findings support the value of separating candidate coverage from conditional ranking performance and explicitly accounting for annotation-density-associated effects when evaluating TF prioritization frameworks.

items.title: Correlative mapping links extracellular matrix architecture to local mechanics in cardiac aging
items.blurb: Cardiac aging is accompanied by extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, but how changes in matrix architecture relate to local tissue mechanics remains poorly understood. Here, we quantified six image-derived architectural descriptors across selected ECM components in young and aged murine myocardium and integrated them into an architectural index that we term 'ArchI'. Age-associated architectural changes differed among ECM components, with higher ArchI values observed for fibrillar collagen, fibronectin, and laminin-associated networks. To examine how defined structural changes affect the component descriptors, we developed controlled synthetic geometries and a stochastic network model. These analyses revealed index sensitivity to matrix occupancy, fiber width, and network continuity.
