Context

It is estimated that since February 2022, around 14 percent of Ukraine’s housing stock has been damaged or destroyed, affecting more than three million households. According to the Fifth Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA5), released in February 2026 and covering the period to 31 December 2025, total direct damage across all sectors has reached approximately USD 195 billion – around 11 percent higher than reported in RDNA4 – with housing remaining the single most affected sector. Housing accounts for roughly 31 percent of total damage, and more than 80 percent of that damage and destruction is concentrated in frontline and border regions.

Throughout 2025 and into early 2026, intensified attacks caused further damage to housing and civilian infrastructure across the east, south and north of the country, increasing the number of people displaced from their homes and in need of thermally insulated shelter. The security situation in Donetska, Kharkivska, Zaporizka and Dnipropetrovska oblasts continued to deteriorate, with evacuations ongoing. Since 1 June 2025, according to government figures, around 150,000 people were evacuated from frontline areas to safer regions, including approximately 18,000 children and more than 5,000 persons with limited mobility; further mandatory evacuations with children from frontline settlements in Donetska, Dnipropetrovska, Zaporizka, Kharkivska and Chernihivska oblasts were ordered in the first half of 2026.

The winter of 2025–2026 was one of the harshest in recent years and proved detrimental to internally displaced persons (IDPs), non-displaced people in war-affected areas, returnees and host communities alike. More than 3.7 million people remained internally displaced, many having been displaced multiple times. The repair and rehabilitation of collective sites are vital life-saving interventions, as the increasing number of displaced persons and repeated re-damage to previously rehabilitated sites continue to outpace available capacity.

Disruptions to centralized and electric heating systems had a profound impact on affected populations during the 2025–2026 season. Between October 2025 and February 2026, coordinated strikes reportedly caused a generation deficit of around 7 GW, and in January 2026 near-daily attacks damaged or destroyed energy assets in at least 17 regions and Kyiv city, leaving millions of people with only a few hours of electricity per day and disrupting heating and water services, particularly in multi-apartment buildings. In early October 2025, the largest attack on Ukraine’s gas infrastructure since the start of the full-scale invasion took an estimated 60 percent of domestic gas production offline. District heating networks remained highly vulnerable – a single damaged facility can interrupt services for entire neighborhoods – and even where infrastructure was operational, heating often remained economically inaccessible due to rising tariffs, irregular income and depleted savings.

Based on operational experience from the 2024–2025 and 2025–2026 winter response seasons, solid fuel remained a critical heating solution in both rural and urban areas. Both in-kind distributions and cash assistance proved effective, with the choice of modality largely determined by market functionality and access constraints. In-kind support was often required in remote and frontline locations where fuel markets were disrupted, access was restricted, or insecurity prevented supplier deliveries. Damage to transport infrastructure further disrupted supply chains and increased delivery costs. Where markets are functioning, cash assistance remains the preferred modality, as it provides households with greater flexibility and dignity in meeting their heating needs. To maximize its effectiveness, cash assistance should be accompanied by clear guidance and communication about its intended purpose and appropriate messaging about heating-related expenditures, including recommended fuel quantities and safe, efficient firewood use.

Given the consistent wintertime targeting of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and the recurring inoperability of heating systems during the coldest months, solid fuel and stoves (including fittings and installation equipment) must continue to be prioritized, irrespective of ongoing price fluctuations. Damage and lack of maintenance have affected heating systems in collective sites and in individual houses and apartments alike; in many cases, these systems – including water heaters, electrical grids, gas and hot-water pipelines, internal pipes, radiators and stoves – must be reactivated, repaired or replaced. Portable heating appliances should be provided where the heating system is dysfunctional or cannot be restored before the upcoming winter season.

One of the most important lessons from the 2025–2026 season is that timing is a core quality standard. Post-distribution monitoring consistently showed that assistance received before the heating season is markedly more effective, whereas delays in implementation and delivery, whether cash transfers or in-kind assistance, forced households to borrow fuel, reduce heating, deplete savings, or purchase at peak prices, and late funding left insufficient lead time for in-kind procurement and delivery. The 2026–2027 response should therefore aim to complete most of the registration, procurement, payments, and in-kind deliveries by October. Lessons learned also reaffirmed the importance of pre-positioning heating appliances and solid fuel in advance of peak winter months, and of giving special attention to female-headed households and elderly individuals, many of whom are unable to physically unload, store or process large firewood deliveries.

In addition to heating, essential household items such as warm winter clothing, thermal underwear and thermal blankets remain necessary for displaced individuals, returnees and others who have lost their belongings, lack access to markets, or cannot afford essential winter items. Interventions should be based on a sex- and age-disaggregated household needs assessment, in line with agreed vulnerability criteria, and may be delivered in-kind or through cash/voucher assistance, wherever feasible and appropriate, particularly for winter preparations.

Assistance continued to be guided by the principle of deduplication. The combined use of winter coordination tables and the RAIS+ platform – used by more than 78 partners – enabled coordinated assistance to over 357,000 households and prevented an estimated USD 45 million in duplicate payments during the 2025–2026 season. Accurate and timely reporting by partners into RAIS+ remains crucial for cross-checking and ensuring harmonized coverage, both within and between clusters.

This guidance is framed within the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP), which estimates that 10.8 million people require humanitarian assistance in 2026 and prioritizes 4.1 million of the most vulnerable. In light of the evolving context and operational lessons from 2025– 2026, the Shelter and NFI Cluster has further adjusted its planning assumptions and priorities for the 2026–2027 winterization response, emphasizing early preparedness, earlier procurement and pre-positioning, stronger and earlier coordination with governmental actors at oblast and hromada levels, improved targeting and deduplication mechanisms, diversified delivery modalities tailored to market constraints, and the explicit integration of energy-shock preparedness. Contextual risks – energy infrastructure disruptions, fluctuating fuel markets and recurring displacement – should be explicitly factored into planning, including pre-positioning in high-risk areas, contingency planning for shifts between cash and in-kind modalities, and flexibility to adapt to changing market and security conditions.

items.title: World: Statement by Principals of the Inter-Agency Standing Committee: Humanitarian Transitions
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Inter-Agency Standing Committee

Please refer to the attached file.

Reset Explained: What Makes a Humanitarian Transition Responsible?

Across many crises, humanitarian needs remain acute while financing and operational presence are contracting. Reductions driven by diminished humanitarian resources or presence are not, in themselves, a responsible transition.

Responsible humanitarian transitions are country-specific. They adapt international assistance and coordination as needs and risks evolve, while sustaining critical protection and assistance and strengthening nationally led and locally grounded pathways to recovery.

On 27 October 2026, IASC Principals affirmed seven principles to guide this collective approach.

What do the seven principles mean in practice?

1. Put people first.
Transitions must protect people's rights and access to essential services, with affected communities meaningfully involved in decisions.

2. Plan early and remain flexible.
Transitions must reflect each context and remain adaptable, including allowing humanitarian assistance to scale back up when needs or protection risks increase.

3. Sustain essential assistance and protection.
Humanitarian responsibilities continue until viable and adequately financed alternatives are in place.

4. Connect humanitarian action with longer-term solutions.
Humanitarian, development and peace actors need to work together, often in parallel, while respecting their different mandates and responsibilities.

5. Strengthen country-level leadership.
Resident and Humanitarian Coordinators, country teams and partners need the support and authority to guide transitions collectively.

6. Let evidence guide decisions.
Shared analysis and transparent benchmarks should track outcomes for people and inform adjustments — not trigger automatic withdrawal.

7. Back transitions with financing.
Timely, flexible and complementary financing is essential to sustain critical services and avoid transferring unfunded responsibilities to communities and partners.

From principles to practice

The test of a responsible transition is what happens to people as humanitarian arrangements change.

Are they still protected? Do essential services continue? Are national and local actors supported to lead? Can humanitarian assistance respond again if needs increase?

The IASC Principals have established the principles. The next step is applying them in each context, with responsibilities, resources and accountability clearly defined.

Read the full IASC Principals' Statement on Humanitarian Transitions, 27 October 2026.

Explore more in Humanitarian Reset: In Action.

items.title: oPt: No conditions for life: Women, girls and the gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza
items.blurb:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: Amnesty International

Please refer to the attached file.

Israel/OPT: Women and girls bear the crushing toll of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza

Israel has relentlessly inflicted repeated and cumulative harms on women and girls in the occupied Gaza Strip since October 2023 as an integral part of its ongoing genocide against Palestinians, said Amnesty International in a new report published today.

No conditions for life: Women, girls and the gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, lays out in 135 pages of harrowing detail, Israel’s ongoing genocide despite the so-called ceasefire of October 2025, providing evidence of how the Israeli military, between 7 October 2023 and 1 October 2026, has repeatedly killed, injured, forcibly displaced, unlawfully detained, deliberately denied women and girls access to essential healthcare, including reproductive healthcare, and starved them. It illustrates how these measures have forced women into a daily struggle for survival defined by grief and trauma and stripped away the conditions necessary for women to exercise autonomy over decisions relating to pregnancy, childbirth and reproductive health.

“Two years ago, Amnesty International published a report concluding unequivocally that Israel is committing genocide, the finding of intensive investigation into Israel’s conduct since 7 October 2023, and in-depth legal analysis of courts decisions on genocide. This new report sheds light on the profound gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide, providing new details about the brutal harms inflicted on women and girls that continue to devastate their lives and cause agonizing suffering despite the so-called ceasefire. Our report further demonstrates that even after the so-called ceasefire between Hamas and Israel in October 2025, Israel has continued to commit genocide, by deliberately inflicting on Palestinians in Gaza conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction and causing serious bodily and mental harm to them,” said Agnès Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International.

“Two years ago, Amnesty International published a report concluding unequivocally that Israel is committing genocide, the finding of intensive investigation into Israel’s conduct since 7 October 2023, and in-depth legal analysis of courts decisions on genocide. This new report sheds light on the profound gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide, providing new details about the brutal harms inflicted on women and girls that continue to devastate their lives and cause agonizing suffering despite the so-called ceasefire. Our report further demonstrates that even after the so-called ceasefire between Hamas and Israel in October 2025, Israel has continued to commit genocide, by deliberately inflicting on Palestinians in Gaza conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction and causing serious bodily and mental harm to them,” said Agnès Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International.

“Over the past three years, Israel has demonstrated an unending calculated intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza. Women and girls in Gaza have endured a relentless assault on every aspect of their lives. They have been killed, injured, displaced, starved and denied access to essential healthcare, while systematically stripped of the conditions necessary to make decisions about pregnancy, childbirth and their reproductive futures. Pre-existing gender inequalities, disproportionate caregiving responsibilities and unmet reproductive healthcare needs have compounded the harms inflicted on women and girls. Israel’s dismantling of social networks and protection systems, including through repeated evacuation orders, has also exposed them to gender-based violence. These violations are not incidental to Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza but are an integral part of it.

Over the past three years, Israel has demonstrated an unending calculated intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza. Women and girls in Gaza have endured a relentless assault on every aspect of their lives. They have been killed, injured, displaced, starved and denied access to essential healthcare, while systematically stripped of the conditions necessary to make decisions about pregnancy, childbirth and their reproductive futures.

Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International

“States have a legal and moral duty to pressure Israel’s government to stop the ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, protect the rights of​​ women and girls and address gendered crimes. They must use all means at their disposal to dismantle the structures enabling Israel’s unlawful occupation and system of apartheid. This includes immediately halting all arms transfers to Israel, imposing targeted sanctions on Israeli officials implicated in genocide and other crimes under international law, and ensuring that businesses do not contribute to or profit from Israel’s unlawful conduct. They must do everything to ensure Israeli officials responsible for crimes are investigated and prosecuted. They must support the International Criminal Court (ICC) in ensuring that caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces the ICC judges.”

Amnesty International’s report also presents evidence that Israel has imposed measures that had, and continue to have, the effect of preventing births among Palestinians in Gaza, and calls for Israel to be investigated for the genocidal act of imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group, as prohibited under Article II(d) of the Genocide Convention, in addition to the other genocidal acts defined under the Convention.

The report is based on 228 interviews conducted between October 2023 and October 2026, including with women and girls, healthcare workers, NGO and UN staff, and other witnesses in Gaza. It is also informed by verified photos and videos, medical records, satellite imagery, and extensive research from Palestinian, Israeli and international sources. Amnesty International shared its findings with the Israeli authorities and the Hamas political bureau on 30 September 2026 but had received no response at the time of publication.

The report sets out multiple and cumulative harms women and girls have been subjected to over three years.

Killings, bereavement and shattered families

Since 7 October 2023, Israel’s attacks have killed and injured Palestinians on a scale exceptional in comparison with 21st century armed conflicts.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza, 22,331 women and girls were among the 74,237 Palestinians killed between 7 October 2023 and 1 October 2026, making up 30.1 per cent of all fatalities. An average of 30 women and girls were killed every day during the first two years of the genocide.

On 29 October 2024, one of the deadliest Israeli air strikes documented by Amnesty International killed 137 people from the Abu Nasr family, including 38 women, 44 men and 55 children, 24 of them girls, as they were sleeping.

Aida, then 15, narrowly survived with life-changing injuries:

“I woke up to the sound of people screaming, my sister dying, my family next to me, all killed. When I regained my consciousness, I could not move, I was beneath the rubble,” she said. “My father was killed, my three brothers, my two sisters, their spouses, their children.”

While the scale of killings decreased after the so-called ceasefire of October 2025, between then and 1 October 2026, Israeli forces had killed 1,439 Palestinians, including 274 women and girls, according to Gaza’s health ministry. Israeli forces also injured over 5,330, including 1,473 women and girls in this period.

Women Amnesty International spoke to across Gaza described still living under a constant threat of death. Palestinians living near the so-called “Yellow Line” areas face a particular risk, as Israeli forces use drone strikes and live fire against civilians to prevent access to these areas. The “Yellow Line” is a shifting military boundary imposed after the ceasefire that left more than half of Gaza under Israeli military control and has since been further expanded.

Women experienced killings and injuries both directly and through the loss of loved ones, often shouldering greater caregiving responsibilities and heading households alone amid acute hardship. For many, pregnancy, childbirth and early motherhood unfolded amid bereavement, trauma, displacement and bombardment.

Dismantling maternal healthcare

Israel’s genocide has decimated Gaza’s health sector rendering scores of healthcare facilities non-functional. Over 90 per cent of Gaza’s hospitals are either destroyed or only partially functional. Medical workers and patients described the remaining maternal healthcare facilities as overwhelmed, with women giving birth while sharing beds or on the floor.

Healthcare professionals have also linked Israel’s unlawful blockade and severe restrictions on humanitarian aid and essential supplies, including medicines, fuel and medical equipment, to miscarriages, stillbirths and other serious pregnancy complications, as well as to compromised care during delivery and, in some cases, maternal death. Newborns were also forced to share incubators and other life-saving equipment, contributing to preventable neonatal deaths.

It’s a fight to survive. If you ask any woman in Gaza about the future, they’ll ask: what future?

Amal Siyyam, Director of the Women’s Affairs Centre in Gaza

Amnesty International has also documented how during Israeli sieges of hospitals – particularly in late 2023 and in 2024 – pregnant women and women recovering from childbirth, including those at high risk of complications or experiencing complications, were repeatedly ordered or forced to flee, interrupting critical healthcare. Medical staff also described working in impossible conditions, performing caesarean sections without electricity, adequate anaesthesia or proper sterilization, and delivering babies while sheltering from attacks in hospital basements during these sieges.

The report records the harrowing experiences of women forced to give birth in unimaginable conditions, including while coming under fire during labour or recovering after delivery. Amnesty International also documented how Israeli attacks on and the siege of Al-Shifa hospital in November 2023 contributed to the death of eight preterm babies, while 31 other babies had their life-sustaining treatment interrupted and were separated from their mothers.

In one emblematic case, in October 2023, an Israeli strike hit the home of Sondos Al-Kurd, who was eight months pregnant, killing her three-year-old daughter, Habiba, and several relatives. She was rushed to Al-Shifa Hospital, where doctors performed an emergency caesarean section and saved her newborn daughter.

Just weeks later when Israeli forces besieged and attacked the hospital medical staff told patients to evacuate and Sondos was forced to leave without her newborn who remained in an incubator in intensive care: “I kept saying, ‘My daughter, my daughter’. They told me: ‘Leave her in the incubator.’” As the siege tightened and electricity, fuel and medical supplies ran out, Sondos Al-Kurd feared she would never see her baby again. Her daughter survived and was evacuated for treatment outside Gaza, but Israeli restrictions kept mother and child separated for more than two years.

Israel justified its systematic attacks on healthcare facilities by claiming they were used as “command and control centres” by Hamas. While Amnesty International documented some instances of misuse of hospitals by Palestinian armed groups and Hamas-affiliated authorities, it did not find evidence substantiating the claims they were used as “command and control centres”. In all circumstances, the presence of armed groups does not release Israel of its obligations under international humanitarian law to take all feasible precautions to spare civilians and to refrain from indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks.

Stripped of control over pregnancy, childbirth and reproductive health

Since October 2023, the destruction of reproductive healthcare, the denial of access to essential medicines and services, displacement and food deprivation have collectively and progressively eroded women’s ability to exercise reproductive autonomy. Israel’s attacks and blockade have also shut down all IVF services in Gaza and effectively denied access to fertility treatment by severely restricting travel for those seeking care outside Gaza. Thousands of embryos and other reproductive material of Palestinian families stored in these facilities was destroyed.

One woman, Azza (name changed) described how after becoming pregnant with twins after undergoing IVF treatment, she later experienced cramps and bleeding after a nearby air strike. She delivered a few weeks later and both babies died shortly after birth. The fertility clinic with her remaining embryos had been destroyed and she has not been able to leave Gaza for treatment elsewhere.

“I felt I had lost everything and felt hopeless… I live in a tent with my husband, my mother-in-law, her daughter and granddaughter. I often sit by myself crying or sleeping,” she told Amnesty International.

At the same time, the widespread trauma women have endured has also pushed women to abandon plans for having children.

Starvation and displacement

Israel’s genocide has also deepened pre-existing inequalities and forced women and girls to shoulder extraordinary burdens amid hunger, displacement, trauma and the destruction of homes and support networks. This has heightened the risks of gender-based violence, exploitation and harmful practices and stripped many women and girls of dignity and control over their lives.

Israeli forces have forcibly displaced more than 90 per cent of Gaza’s population since October 2023, often multiple times and under life-threatening conditions. Almost all remain displaced. Amnesty International continued to document new forced displacement after the so-called ceasefire, particularly as Israeli forces have expanded the “Yellow Line” area further into Gaza.

Amal, 58, who had already been displaced four times, described how her family were forced to flee their home east of Deir al-Balah in August 2026 under fire as Israeli tanks advanced. By violently imposing access restrictions including areas behind the “Yellow Line”, Israel is now forcing nearly the entire population of Gaza to live in less than 35 per cent of its land area

For women and girls, displacement has meant the loss of privacy, dignity and autonomy as they struggle to access basic services, manage menstrual hygiene, care for children, and protect themselves in overcrowded shelters. Pregnant, post-partum and older women, particularly those with disabilities or chronic illnesses, faced additional difficulties. Ola described struggling to walk 14km while recovering from a caesarean section the day her 14-year-old son and other family members were killed.

The forced evacuation of Gaza’s domestic violence shelters, and the collapse of protection systems, have left many women and girls with nowhere to seek safety leaving them at heightened risks of exploitation and child marriages.

At the same time, Israel’s ongoing restrictions on humanitarian aid and essential supplies have driven catastrophic levels of hunger and deprivation. While there has been an increase in the quantities of food entering Gaza since the so-called ceasefire of October 2025, restrictions and deprivation persisted. Women interviewed in mid-2026 repeatedly told Amnesty International that they routinely skipped meals so their children could eat and were often unable to obtain nutritious food, infant formula or essential supplies. Pregnant and breastfeeding women faced heightened health risks linked to malnutrition.

Amina (name changed), interviewed in March 2026, described the struggle to keep her family alive after her husband’s disappearance, and while she struggles with health concerns: “My situation is so miserable. We depend on the community kitchens to eat… I can’t afford to buy food, new clothes, or any necessities for my children. I stopped going to look for aid so that I don’t get exploited or harassed.” She added that her eight-year-old daughter is sometimes forced to go out to collect scraps when she is in too much pain to do so herself.

Detention and torture

At least 85 women from Gaza were detained without charge or trial, mostly in the months after 7 October 2023. Women Amnesty International spoke to after release described being subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including severe psychological abuse as well as repeated strip searches, sexualised insults and threats of rape, which amount to sexual violence.

Hundreds of women have been left searching for missing or disappeared loved ones they believed could be in Israeli detention, some until now.

Genocide

Israel is continuing to commit genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, at a minimum through the ongoing deliberate infliction of conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction and through causing serious bodily and mental harm to members of the group.

It is doing this in particular through its continued unlawful blockade on essential items entering Gaza, and on Palestinians’ ability to enter and exit Gaza, and through its violent expansion and maintenance of access-restricted zones across over 65% of Gaza.

In addition, the report found that measures imposed by Israel prevented access to fertility treatment, created trauma and fear for the future that led some women to abandon plans to have children and contributed to miscarriages, stillbirths, and prevented pregnancies resulting in live births. These were the foreseeable outcome of policies and practices maintained and repeated by Israel despite repeated warnings from the UN and humanitarian organizations and in defiance of binding orders by the International Court of Justice.

While Amnesty International could not reach a definitive conclusion regarding whether Israel had imposed these measures with the intent to prevent births among Palestinians in Gaza, as specified in Article II(d) of the Genocide Convention, its pattern of conduct raises serious concerns that this was its intent. The organization is therefore calling for Israel to also be investigated for the additional genocidal act of imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group.

Israel’s genocide in Gaza is not only devastating all aspects of women’s lives but is also destroying hope.

Amal Siyyam, Director of the Women’s Affairs Centre in Gaza told Amnesty International: “It’s a fight to survive. If you ask any woman in Gaza about the future, they’ll ask: what future?”

“Women and girls in Gaza deserve more than just to survive, they deserve a future. As Israeli authorities continue to inflict conditions of life designed to physically destroy Palestinians in Gaza, they are obstructing reconstruction, keeping nearly the entire population displaced and restricting the entry of essential supplies. It is more critical than ever for states to press Israel to lift its blockade and ensure unhindered humanitarian access,” said Agnès Callamard.

“With Israel also perpetrating the genocidal act of causing serious bodily or mental harm, states must also urgently act to support the humanitarian, human rights and women’s groups whose vital work is being hindered by sanctions, deregistration and other restrictions, as they strive to protect human rights and save lives amid this engineered humanitarian catastrophe.”

items.title: No one is spared: The impact of attacks on civilians and healthcare in southern Lebanon [EN/AR]
items.blurb:
Country: Lebanon
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Please refer to the attached files.

Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon inflict severe harm on civilians and healthcare

  • MSF’s latest report documents the lasting impact of Israeli attacks on civilians and healthcare in southern Lebanon.
  • The report, No one is spared, is grounded in direct witnessing by MSF teams who provided care at hospitals in southern Lebanon.
  • Israel must respect and protect medical staff, ambulances, emergency responders, and civilians.

Beirut — Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is releasing a report documenting the detrimental and lasting impact of Israeli attacks on civilians and healthcare in southern Lebanon. While supporting hospitals and first responders during the most recent escalation of Israeli attacks earlier in 2026, MSF teams witnessed first-hand the human and medical cost civilians have borne, and the serious damage inflicted on healthcare.

No one is spared is an evidence-based report grounded in direct witnessing from southern Lebanon, during a period in which MSF supported the provision of emergency and trauma care at Jabal Amel hospital, in Sour (Tyre), and Najdeh Al-Shaabiyeh hospital, in Nabatiyeh. The report captures how Israeli strikes killed or maimed children, elderly people, or entire families. At a time of heightened medical and humanitarian needs, and under pressure of repeated influxes of mass casualties, medical facilities and ambulances were directly struck or affected by Israeli attacks.

All parties to the conflict must uphold their responsibilities under international humanitarian law. Specifically, MSF calls on Israel to respect and protect medical staff, ambulances, emergency responders, and civilians; and to refrain from attacking them, including those who remain in or return to war-affected areas. States with influence over the parties to the conflict must use their diplomatic and political leverage to ensure these obligations are upheld and that attacks affecting civilians and healthcare are addressed.

Devastating and life-altering injuries

Inside emergency rooms and operating theatres, MSF teams and the hospital staff they support treated patients with severe blast, fragmentation, and other traumatic injuries. They treated injuries caused by explosive weapons: internal organ and brain damage caused by extreme pressure waves; fractures, traumatic brain injuries, and penetrating wounds caused by shrapnel; blunt trauma from people being thrown by explosions; and severe burns, crush injuries, and smoke inhalation.

“Our teams witnessed people devastated by the full spectrum of blast trauma,” says Dr Luna Hammad, MSF medical coordinator in Lebanon. “Patients arrived with deep internal damage, shattered bones, and dozens of metallic fragments embedded throughout their bodies. Such injuries overwhelm both the human body and the emergency teams fighting to save lives.”

Our teams witnessed people devastated by the full spectrum of blast trauma... Such injuries overwhelm both the human body and the emergency teams fighting to save lives.

Dr Luna Hammad, MSF medical coordinator in Lebanon

Many of these injuries pointed to specific weapons used in the strikes. Lebanese Civil Defence teams reported three types of drone-fired munitions: standard explosives, munitions fitted with blades, and munitions packed with small metallic cubes. MSF medical staff treated wounds consistent with all three — most frequently high-velocity shrapnel from metallic cubes tearing through multiple body parts.

Surviving an attack is only the beginning of an arduous recovery. Many patients required multiple complex surgical operations and prolonged intensive care, and will need further surgeries, physical rehabilitation, prosthetic devices, and ongoing medical follow-up. Yet, accessing this care remains acutely difficult for many people.

The escalation of Israeli attacks in early 2026 strained a health system already grappling with shortages of specialised staff and medical supplies, forcing the reduction or suspension of non-emergency care and complicating referrals to specialised facilities.

The medical mission was not spared

As civilian casualties mounted, the healthcare system itself came under attack. MSF documented incidents in which Israeli strikes directly hit, or landed dangerously close to, medical facilities, ambulances, and rescue teams. A single Israeli strike in the vicinity of Jabal Amel hospital, on 1 June 2026, injured 127 people, including 39 health workers, marking the highest number of health workers wounded in a single attack during the escalation.
MSF teams also witnessed the impact on healthcare workers first-hand, with paramedics and health workers arriving at hospitals injured or killed following attacks. This included incidents in which first responders were reportedly struck while attempting to rescue or recover casualties from previous attacks.

“Irreplaceable people whose knowledge and courage saved lives were killed while providing care where it’s needed most,” says Guilherme Botelho, MSF head of mission in Lebanon. “Their deaths are not an unavoidable tragedy, but the direct, human cost of attacks on healthcare. They were mothers, fathers, colleagues, and pillars of their communities who remained in war-affected areas at grave personal risk, and we are all forced to mourn them.”

Despite the lack of protection guarantees and severe operational constraints, paramedics and hospital staff in southern Lebanon continued to deliver care and serve their communities. Because teams had to wait until it was safe for them to go and navigate severe risks to rescuers, lifesaving responses were repeatedly delayed or restricted.

These delays left emergency teams with less time to stabilise patients at the scene, complicated ambulance transport, and prolonged the time victims remained trapped under rubble. Ambulances were at times forced to transport multiple patients at once, while hospitals absorbed sudden waves of mass casualties with limited staff, supplies, and referral options. The fallout extended far beyond emergency departments, diverting scarce resources and disrupting routine care for surrounding communities.

MSF is deeply alarmed by the severe human and medical cost of Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon, affecting civilians and healthcare. International humanitarian law is not optional. Civilians and healthcare must be protected in conflicts, in southern Lebanon and around the world.

Notes to editors

MSF is an international, independent medical humanitarian organisation that provides medical assistance to people affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, and exclusion from healthcare. Our teams are made up of tens of thousands of health professionals, logistics, and administrative staff, bound together by our charter. Our actions are guided by medical ethics and the principles of impartiality, independence, and neutrality.

In Lebanon, following the escalation of Israeli attacks on 2 March 2026, MSF scaled up our nationwide emergency response to support the Lebanese health system and address the needs of war-affected communities.

Between March and June 2026, MSF mobile medical teams provided essential general healthcare services, including mental health care, to displaced people and other conflict-affected communities across Beirut, Mount Lebanon, Bekaa, Baalbek-Hermel, North, Nabatiyeh, and South governorates. MSF teams also provided referrals when needed, supported community kitchens, distributed essential relief items (mattresses, blankets, hygiene kits, and more), and provided water and sanitation services through water trucking, rehabilitating water networks and sanitation facilities, and installing water treatment systems.

items.title: GIEWS Country Brief: Morocco 24-November-2026
items.blurb:
Country: Morocco
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

FOOD SECURITY SNAPSHOT

  1. Planting of 2027 winter cereals underway amid improved water availability
  2. Cereal production rebounded sharply in 2026
  3. Cereal import requirements forecast at below‑average level in 2026/27
  4. Annual food inflation increased slightly in October 2026

Planting of 2027 winter cereals underway amid improved water availability

Planting of the 2027 winter wheat and barley crops started at the beginning of November. To support domestic agricultural production, the government announced the distribution of subsidized seeds and the provision of fertilizers. The 2026/27 season started with improved availability of irrigation water, reflecting the abundant rainfall during the previous season. As of early November, national reservoirs were filled to nearly 66 percent of capacity, compared with about 30 percent a year earlier. Although improved water availability could support an expansion of irrigated cereal area, most cereal production remains rainfed. Seasonal forecasts indicate above‑average precipitation between December 2026 and February 2027 in northwestern parts of the country, potentially supporting crop establishment and early development. Nevertheless, production prospects for the 2027 cereal crops will continue to largely depend on the timing and distribution of rainfall during the remainder of the growing season.

Cereal production rebounded sharply in 2026

Total cereal production in 2026 is estimated at about 9 million tonnes, nearly 70 percent above the five‑year average and almost double the drought‑affected 2025 output. The sharp recovery reflects favourable weather conditions as abundant rainfall amounts from November 2025 onwards restored soil moisture levels and replenished water reservoirs, supporting crop development throughout the growing season.

Cereal import requirements forecast at below‑average level in 2026/27

Cereal import requirements in the 2026/27 marketing year (July/June) are forecast at 7.5 million tonnes, about 22 percent below the average, largely reflecting the above‑average 2026 wheat output. Wheat import requirements are expected at 3.5 million tonnes, about 40 percent below the average. Despite the expected decline, the country remains heavily reliant on imports to meet domestic cereal consumption needs. Following the temporary introduction of higher import duties during the harvest period, the government reintroduced subsidies for soft wheat imports from mid‑September until 31 December 2026, with the aim of facilitating imports, ensuring adequate domestic supplies and stabilizing prices.

Annual food inflation increased slightly in October 2026

Food inflation increased slightly by 0.3 percent year‑on‑year in October 2026, marking the first annual increase after five consecutive months of declines. On a monthly basis, food prices increased by 1.6 percent, mainly driven by higher prices of meat, vegetables, dairy products and eggs.

items.title: GIEWS Country Brief: The Oriental Republic of Uruguay 24-November-2026
items.blurb:
Country: Uruguay
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

FOOD SECURITY SNAPSHOT

  1. Below‑average wheat output expected in 2026 due to reduced plantings
  2. Cereal exports in 2026/27 forecast slightly below average
  3. Prices of wheat and maize higher than one year earlier in September

Below‑average wheat output expected in 2026 due to reduced plantings

Harvesting of the 2026 wheat crop started in November and production is preliminary forecast below average at 1.2 million tonnes. According to the latest official estimates, the area planted declined from the previous year and is estimated at 268 540 hectares, about 7 percent below the five‑year average. Lower year‑on‑year prices and rising production costs ahead of the planting period in April 2026 reduced profit margins and discouraged wheat sowings. In addition, high humidity associated with abundant precipitation negatively affected flowering and development phases in localized areas. Excessive soil moisture also increased the risk of fusariosis outbreaks, further curbing yield prospects.

Planting of the 2027 paddy and maize crops is nearing completion under generally favourable weather conditions. The area planted to paddy, concentrated mainly in eastern regions, is preliminarily estimated above the five‑year average, supported by steady export demand and improved access to credit through the approval of a credit facility in September 2026 of about USD 50 million, targeting around 400 producers. However, paddy sowings declined from the previous year, reflecting lower profitability amid reduced prices and rising production costs. The area planted to maize is anticipated at record‑high level, underpinned by strong domestic demand from the feed industry and lower expected returns from soybeans, which encouraged farmers to shift acreage towards maize.

Weather forecasts point to high likelihood of above‑average precipitation amounts between December 2026 and February 2027, associated with El Niño event, likely benefiting paddy and maize crop development.

Cereal exports in 2026/27 forecast slightly below average

Cereal exports in 2026/27 marketing year (April/March) are forecast at 2.2 million tonnes, slightly below the five‑year average, reflecting reduced exportable surpluses of wheat and rice. Cereal import requirements are preliminary forecast at near‑average levels in 2026/27 as stable maize import needs are expected to be largely met by domestic production.

Prices of wheat and maize higher than one year earlier in September

Wholesale prices of yellow maize strengthened seasonally in August and September 2026, when they were about 50 percent above their year‑earlier levels. The surge reflected tight supply following to the drought‑affected 2026 harvest, the smallest in three years, as well as rising international prices.

Prices of wheat grains, predominantly supplied by domestic production, were stable in August 2026, but increased by 10 percent month‑on‑month in September. The increase reflected concerns about the impact of excessive precipitation on crop flowering and early‑development stages. In September, wheat prices were about 20 percent above their year‑earlier levels, also supported by rising international prices linked to logistical disruptions in the Black Sea Region.

Rice prices declined steadily between March and October 2026, when they were almost 15 percent lower than one year before, supported by ample market supplies following two consecutive years of above‑average production.

items.blurb:
Country: Malawi
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

21-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

Based on information available as of 21 October 2026, multiple forecasting and food security analyses indicate an elevated risk of severe drought impacts across southern Malawi and parts of the central region during the 2026/27 agricultural season. The latest FEWS NET Food Security Outlook projects worsening food security outcomes and estimates that between 1.5 and 1.99 million people may require humanitarian assistance should forecast conditions materialize, with needs expected to peak between January and March 2027.

These projections are supported by the 2026/27 Seasonal Climate Outlook issued by the Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS), which forecasts delayed rainfall onset, prolonged dry spells, below-normal rainfall, and heightened drought risk across much of southern Malawi. Earlier regional analyses, including the ROSEA El Niño Preparedness Alert, also identified Malawi among countries facing increased risk of drought-related impacts associated with a strong El Niño event.

Taken together, these forecasts present a strong evidence base for anticipatory action before humanitarian impacts escalate. The anticipated consequences include reduced agricultural production, declining household income, reduced access to water, increased food insecurity, deterioration of nutrition outcomes, and heightened vulnerability among households with limited coping capacity.

In response to these forecast triggers, Malawi Red Cross Society (MRCS) seeks support through the DREF to implement anticipatory actions in five high-risk districts: Chikwawa, Balaka, Neno, Blantyre, and Mulanje. The operation will focus on protecting livelihoods, strengthening preparedness, improving household water security, promoting early action behaviour, and reducing the anticipated humanitarian impacts of drought before conditions worsen. Monitoring and rapid assessments will be used to track evolving risks and support operational decision-making throughout implementation.

Ces données ont été collecté pendant l'évaluation des besoins rapide, suite aux dégâts enregistrés après les pluies diluviennes du 10 et 11 novembre 2026 à Brazzaville et Pointe-Noire. Cf. le rapport d'évaluation

Description

Dans la nuit du 10 au 11 novembre 2026, des pluies torrentielles d'une intensité exceptionnelle se sont abattues sur les deux principales agglomérations de la République du Congo, à savoir Brazzaville et Pointe-Noire. L'engorgement des collecteurs d'eaux pluviales, le débordement des cours d'eau urbains et le ruissellement sur des sols déjà saturés ont provoqué des inondations soudaines et d'importants dégâts matériels dans plusieurs quartiers vulnérables.

Dès le 12 novembre 2026, la Croix-Rouge Congolaise (CRC), à travers ses équipes nationales d'intervention (NDRT) et les volontaires des branches départementales de Brazzaville et de Pointe-Noire, a déployé une mission d'évaluation rapide multisectorielle. La méthodologie a combiné :

  1. des entretiens avec les informateurs clés (chefs de quartiers, chefs de zones, services sociaux municipaux),
  2. des observations directes des dommages sur les habitations et infrastructures hydrauliques,
  3. des discussions de groupe focalisées (FGD) séparées avec les femmes, les hommes, les jeunes et les personnes vivant avec un handicap, et
  4. un dénombrement rapide porte-à-porte des ménages sinistrés.

L'évaluation rapide a permis de recenser un total de 2 300 ménages directement victimes des inondations, représentant environ 13 800 personnes affectées. Parmi ces ménages, 650 ont subi la destruction totale ou l'effondrement de leur habitation et 1 650 ont enregistré une inondation sévère avec perte de biens essentiels

items.title: Kenya Flood 2026 - DREF Final Report (MDRKE070)
items.blurb:
Country: Kenya
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date of event

06-03-2026

What happened, where and when?

Kenya experienced an early and unusually intense onset of the March–May (MAM) long rains beginning in early February 2026, driven by enhanced convective activity across the Lake Victoria basin, the Highlands West and East of the Rift Valley, and the southeastern lowlands.

Throughout the first two weeks of February, heavy precipitation progressively saturated soils and swelled major river basins across the Western, Rift Valley, Central, Nairobi, Lower Eastern, and parts of the North Eastern regions. Simultaneously, the Coastal region experienced severe windstorms alongside downstream flooding caused by heavy runoff draining from the central and southeastern highlands.

By 16 February 2026, the compounding effects of sustained rainfall pushed river systems past critical thresholds, triggering widespread flash floods and prompting the Kenya Red Cross Society (KRCS) to mobilize a national emergency response. Between mid-February and early March, persistent downpours, overflowing rivers, and localized mudslides caused widespread fatalities, population displacement, destruction of homes, loss of livestock and livelihoods, and the severing of key road networks across multiple counties.

The crisis escalated sharply on 6 March 2026, when an intense, six-hour evening cloudburst beginning at approximately 1830 hours overwhelmed drainage systems across Nairobi and its surrounding metropolitan areas. Preceded by weeks of continuous rain that had already pushed Nairobi’s cumulative seasonal rainfall past 534 mm, the storm dumped unprecedented volumes within a three-to-five hour window—recording 160 mm at Wilson Airport, 145 mm at Moi Air Base, 117 mm at Kabete, and 112 mm in Dagoretti.

With the ground fully saturated and urban waterways bursting their banks, the resulting flash floods washed away bridges, submerged informal settlements and low-lying neighborhoods, and rendered major arterial roads impassable, displacing hundreds of residents overnight. The combined destruction of critical infrastructure, loss of property, and disruption of essential services severely compounded the ongoing humanitarian emergency. By the wake of the 6 March deluge, the nationwide death toll had climbed to 53 people, including 27 fatalities recorded in Nairobi in a single night. A summary of the rapid needs assessment conducted by KRCS is mentioned in the shelter section.

items.title: They belong to Jerusalem’s past and present: meet the African Palestinians
items.blurb:
Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited

  • Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure.

There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem.

items.title: 8 Simple Ways Our Grandparents Kept Their Homes Warm in Winter Without Using Room Heaters
items.blurb: Cold floors, chilly corners, and the familiar hunt for a sunny spot in the house are all part of winter. Growing up, many of us watched our grandparents prepare for the season by bringing out thick cotton razais , spreading handwoven durries , and opening curtains to let the afternoon sun in. These simple habits can still help us stay comfortable, reduce electricity bills, and make better use of things we already own. Here are eight traditional and sustainable ways to keep your home warmer this winter without constantly relying on a room heater. 1. Make the most of the winter sun Open curtains and shutters in rooms that receive direct sunlight during the day. Let sunlight fall on floors, walls, and furniture. Once evening approaches, draw the curtains to reduce the chill coming through windows. Cold floors, chilly corners, and the familiar hunt for a sunny spot in the house are all part of winter. Photograph: (Architectural Digest) Thicker curtains can provide an additional layer between the room and cold window panes. This is a humble form of passive solar heating. Traditional homes in our country were often designed around local climates, using natural light, ventilation, and locally available materials. Vernacular architecture in India offers useful examples of how traditional building designs work with natural conditions to create comfortable living spaces. 2. Bring out the traditional razais and quilts A well-filled cotton razai , woollen blanket, or quilt can make a bed comfortable without consuming electricity. Layer a lighter blanket beneath a thicker quilt on particularly cold nights. Keep an additional throw near the sofa for chilly evenings. Instead of replacing bedding every winter, air it on a dry, sunny day and repair loose seams or worn covers. Store it only when completely dry, preferably in a clean cotton bag. Reusing and maintaining bedding helps extend its life and reduces unnecessary purchases. 3. Cover cold floors with durries and rugs Stone and tiled floors can feel particularly cold during winter mornings. Place cotton durries, woollen rugs, or existing carpets in frequently used areas, such as beside the bed, near the sofa, and in a reading corner. Place cotton durries, woollen rugs, or existing carpets in frequently used areas. Photograph: (Amazon.in) You do not need to cover the entire floor. A few strategically placed rugs can make everyday spaces more comfortable. If you already own a handwoven durrie, bring it out instead of purchasing a new synthetic carpet. Shake it outdoors regularly and keep it dry to prevent dampness and unpleasant smells. 4. Layer clothing with natural fabrics A woollen sweater, shawl, socks, and comfortable slippers can make sitting in a chilly room considerably more pleasant. Wear a few layers that can be added or removed as temperatures change. Woollen garments and hand-me-downs can last for several years when cared for properly. If you need something new, consider repairing an old garment or buying a durable piece from a local maker instead of choosing something that may only last one season. 5. Use old fabric to block cold air Cold air can enter through gaps beneath doors and around windows. Instead of buying plastic draught stoppers, repurpose old household textiles. Roll an old towel or stitch leftover cotton fabric into a long cushion and place it beneath doors to limit cold air entering from outside. Check window frames for gaps and use suitable removable sealing strips where necessary. However, avoid blocking ventilation openings, particularly in kitchens and bathrooms, as homes need adequate airflow. 6. Spend more time in one sunny room Rather than trying to keep every room equally warm, arrange your daily activities in the part of the house that receives the most sunlight. If you already own a handwoven durrie, bring it out instead of purchasing a new synthetic carpet. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) Move a chair, work desk, or floor cushion closer to a sunny spot during the day. Close doors to rooms that are not being used, particularly those that remain noticeably colder. This helps you make better use of naturally available warmth without needing additional appliances. 7. Take inspiration from traditional Himalayan homes Traditional homes in colder parts of the country provide useful lessons in sustainable construction. In Himachal Pradesh, Kath-Kuni houses use alternating layers of stone and timber , with thick walls and mud plaster. Their construction helps insulate interiors and retain warmth. The revival of Kath-Kuni architecture in Himachal Pradesh shows how traditional building techniques and locally available materials can preserve architectural knowledge. Similarly, homes in Ladakh have traditionally used mud, stone, willow, and poplar to respond to the region’s harsh winters. Traditional building techniques in Ladakh offer examples of how natural materials can be incorporated into contemporary homes. While these construction techniques cannot directly be replicated in apartments, they demonstrate the importance of choosing materials and designs suited to local climates. 8. Keep your home dry and ventilated Damp rooms can feel colder and may encourage mould growth. Dry wet clothes outdoors when the weather permits, wipe condensation from windows, and use kitchen and bathroom exhaust fans when cooking or bathing. A woollen sweater, shawl, socks, and comfortable slippers can make sitting in a chilly room considerably more pleasant. Photograph: (Pexels) Open windows briefly when outdoor conditions are suitable to allow fresh air to circulate. Keeping a home warm should not mean sealing it completely. Adequate ventilation is important for maintaining a healthy indoor environment. A warmer home through mindful choices Keeping your home comfortable during winter does not always require expensive appliances or renovations. Traditional architecture also offers lessons in building homes that respond to their surroundings. By combining these practices with mindful consumption, households can stay comfortable while reducing unnecessary energy use. These measures may not replace safe heating during severe cold , but they can reduce the need to rely on room heaters constantly.

items.title: Peepal Baba, Who’s Planted 2.5 Crore Trees, Explains What Mumbai Loses When It Cuts 25-Year-Old Trees
items.blurb: Last week, on 19th November, 2026, a video started doing the rounds on social media. You may have seen it. A woman is standing in a park in Mumbai, crying. Around her, workers are cutting down trees. One of them is a big old banyan. The workers say it is about 35 years old. She shakes her head — it has been here much longer than that, she says. “This is our tree. This is not their tree to cut.” The woman is Pooja Ruparel. If you have watched Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge , you will remember her as the little girl in the film. The park is Nana-Nani Park in Versova. On 18 November, Mumbai’s civic body, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), started cutting trees there to make room for part of a new coastal road. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pooja Ruparel (@poojaruparel) Pooja shared the clips on Instagram. Before long, news websites were writing about them. Actors like Dia Mirza and Richa Chadha spoke up too. People have not stopped talking about it since. Not everyone sees it the same way. Some people felt her pain. Others asked: what will crying change? Doesn’t a crowded city like Mumbai need new roads? Pooja says the tree was protected and cutting it was illegal. The BMC says it had every permission it needed. But set the arguments aside for a moment, and the video leaves you with a few simple questions. What do we really lose when a tree that has grown for 25 years is cut down? Can’t we just dig it up and plant it somewhere else? And does building a road always have to mean losing a park? Scientists have actually tried to answer the first question. It takes roughly 400 saplings to do the work of one old tree. That is the estimate of Andreas Roloff, a forestry scientist at TU Dresden in Germany. To match the shade, cooling, air filtration and carbon storage of a single mature tree with a 20-metre crown, he calculated, a city would need to plant around 400 young ones. Researchers at the Technical University of Munich arrived at a similar conclusion from another direction: when an old city tree is replaced with a young one, the tree count stays the same, but often more than 90 per cent of its benefits disappear. India has tried to put a number on it, too. In 2021, an expert committee appointed by the Supreme Court valued a tree at ₹74,500 for every year it lives — counting the oxygen, biofertiliser, compost and micronutrients it gives away free — and observed that an old tree and a fresh sapling are simply not equivalent. Those figures have been tested on the ground in Mumbai this past week. Despite of many efforts by our community members to save Nana Nani Park, the trees there are being cut. Mumbai already lacks third places for people to hangout, Mumbai’s Air is unbreathable. Yet they want to make it worse! There seems no end to this destruction! https://t.co/61pIJNHNmw — Save Mumbai Mangroves (@MumbaiMangroves) November 18, 2026 On 18 November 2026, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) began felling trees at Nana-Nani Park in Versova to make way for an interchange on the Coastal Road North (Versova–Bhayandar) project. Under the approved plan, 184 trees in the park are to be cut and another 164 transplanted to Seven Bungalows nearby. Around 44 were reportedly brought down on the first day. The park was built in 2001 on what had been a dumping ground. Residents planted and tended its trees for 25 years; many of them have spoken of raising those trees like children. Videos of the felling — including the loss of an old banyan — spread quickly, and protests followed. More than 3,200 objections had been filed with the civic body earlier in the year, and residents had proposed an alternative alignment. The BMC maintains that all permissions were obtained and that the felling and compensatory plantation plans were cleared by its Tree Authority. There is one more detail worth knowing. Under Maharashtra’s 2021 amendment to its urban tree law, only trees estimated to be 50 years or older are classified as “heritage trees” and given special protection. Most of Nana-Nani Park’s trees, at around 25, fall well short of that line. Swami Prem Parivartan thinks the line is drawn in the wrong place. Better known as Peepal Baba, and often called India’s Tree Father, he planted his first sapling in 1977, at the age of 11, at the urging of a schoolteacher. Nearly five decades later, he and his Give Me Trees Trust have planted and preserved more than 2.5 crore trees across over 200 districts in India. He spoke to The Better India about what Mumbai stands to lose — and what it could still choose to do differently. ‘Any tree older than 20 years should be a protected living form’ Nana-Nani Park is losing 184 established trees, most of them mature. Ecologically, what does it mean for one neighbourhood to lose that many trees at once? “Any tree that is more than 20 years old should, I believe, be recognised as a protected entity. It should be considered a protected living form. Nana-Nani Park is not an isolated case. Similar disputes have surfaced in Nashik, around Bhimashankar, in Uttarakhand and across north India. Photograph: (Instagram/@navneetmishraa) “There are so many ecosystem services associated with a tree. This is not just about timber. Trees provide shelter and shade, help with carbon sequestration, and support pollinators such as bees, birds and butterflies. They provide nesting and roosting spaces, retain moisture, prevent soil erosion and support the microbial populations that live around their roots. They also help create microclimates wherever they grow.” In other words, a neighbourhood that loses 184 trees does not lose 184 objects. It loses 184 small systems — each one sheltering, cooling, feeding and holding soil in place for everything around it. ‘You cannot protect yourselves if you destroy the elders of the natural world’ In a city as dense as Mumbai, surrounded by concrete, roads and buildings, how important are mature trees? And what happens to the birds and insects that have built their lives around them? For Peepal Baba, a tree that has stood for two or three decades has become part of the community’s living fabric. Birds roost in it, insects feed on it, and a web of soil microbes depends on its roots. Remove it, he says, and those relationships do not simply relocate. “Trees are a very important part of biodiversity. You cannot preserve your culture, or even protect yourselves, if you keep cutting down, chopping up, eliminating and destroying the elders of the natural world — while thinking that compensatory afforestation will somehow make up for it.” The science on heat backs the urgency. A recent study from Northwestern University tracking Chicago’s tree canopy found that the near-term health benefits of tree cover come largely from big trees already standing, and that protecting existing canopy may do more good than planting alone. A sapling planted today will take decades to cast the shade that a 25-year-old tree casts now. Nana-Nani Park’s trees were planted by people who are now grandparents themselves. They watched the saplings grow into a canopy over 25 years. Photograph: (Instagram/@navneetmishraa) It is also why he is uneasy with replanting that happens far away. For the Coastal Road North project as a whole, the BMC’s compensatory plantation of more than 19,500 trees is planned in Panvel, citing a lack of space within Mumbai. His view is simple: “If trees are cut down somewhere, the same species should be planted as close as possible to the location where they were removed.” The work you don’t see in a park When we look at a city park, we usually see trees and benches. What less visible ecological processes are going on inside an established green space? Much of what an old tree does happens out of sight, Peepal Baba explains — in the soil around its roots, in the moisture it holds, and in the cooler pocket of air beneath its canopy. These are the processes that take years to establish and cannot be planted overnight. “Wherever a tree grows, it creates a microclimate. It retains moisture. Its roots hold the soil together and support an entire microbial population. Bees, birds and butterflies come to it. So many forms of life depend on one tree.” That matters in a city built on reclaimed land and battered by monsoon flooding and rising heat. Shade lowers surface temperatures. Roots slow run-off. Canopy catches rain before it hits the ground. In Nana-Nani Park, all of this was being done quietly, for free, by trees that residents had planted on a former garbage dump. ‘Transplanting sounds wonderful. In most cases, the tree does not survive.’ Under the plan, 164 trees will be transplanted. Residents had also suggested relocating mature trees rather than felling them. Is transplantation a real alternative? This is where Peepal Baba is most emphatic. “There is something people find very appealing to hear: that a tree has been uprooted from one place and planted somewhere else. It sounds like a wonderful solution. But scientifically, the success rate is extremely low.” He points out that countries such as Japan, Germany, Switzerland, Italy and France have had better results — but with different climates, better technology and, crucially, years of committed aftercare. “In India, when a tree is uprooted and moved to another location, nobody even goes back to check on it. Nobody ensures that it is watered. Even if you instruct a contractor to move a tree, once the two- or three-month tender period ends, the contractor will not return to maintain it. They will not make sure it gets water or manure, or that it is protected from cows, buffaloes, goats, nilgai — and human beings. In most cases, the tree simply does not survive.” Mumbai’s own records suggest he has reason to be sceptical. In 2020, the city’s municipal commissioner admitted before the Bombay High Court that only about 36 per cent of trees transplanted for the Metro III line had survived after two years. A later RTI analysis by the Watchdog Foundation found that of 6,043 trees transplanted across the city’s wards, 4,444 had died. Mumbaikars are speaking, are you listening. Today at Nana Nani Park people gathered to demand that @mybmc stop the cutting and where the 48 trees will be transplanted, if it will be an actual transplantation, not sapling-tokenism and independently review the alternative before causing irreversible damage. #savenanananipark — Save Mumbai Mangroves (@MumbaiMangroves) November 21, 2026 Which is why, he says, the debate should shift altogether: “At least in our country, uprooting a tree and planting it somewhere else should not even be considered a viable argument . The discussion should be about protecting the trees that already exist.” If removal is truly unavoidable, he says, the replacement should be the same species, planted as close as possible, at the greatest height and maturity possible, with the largest root ball. And if anything must be moved, it should be the young. “If it is a relatively new plantation — trees that are two, three, four or five years old — then perhaps those can be removed. That may still be manageable. But a large, old tree simply cannot adjust to being uprooted.” ‘Trees are not anti-development’ Nana-Nani Park has become shorthand for infrastructure versus ecology. How do you see that debate? Peepal Baba rejects the framing entirely. “The debate should not be about infrastructure versus ecology, or infrastructure versus old trees. If you want to build infrastructure, you must also acknowledge the life-giving features of the natural world, and the enormous role trees play in it. “Trees are not anti-development. They are not anti-infrastructure. Build your infrastructure, by all means. But do it with a little sensitivity, compassion and empathy. Please do not touch the old trees.” He argues the two are not just compatible but dependent on each other — and that the market already knows it. “The beauty and value of a landscape , including its real estate value, rises when there are beautiful trees around, when there is water, when there are flowers, and when birds, bees and butterflies are present. Both can coexist. In fact, they are interdependent.” Nana-Nani Park is not an isolated case. Similar disputes have surfaced in Nashik, around Bhimashankar, in Uttarakhand and across north India. Each time, he says, the same question returns: was every alternative examined before the oldest trees were marked? The grandparents in the village When asked why an old tree can’t simply start over somewhere new, Peepal Baba reaches for an image anyone can recognise. “It is like saying we should uproot our grandparents, or our parents, who have spent their entire lives in one village. Their culture, their habits, their society, their friends and relatives — all of it is rooted in that one place. You cannot simply move them and settle them in another village. That is not how life works. They would die a slow death. “The same thing happens to trees.” Nana-Nani Park’s trees were planted by people who are now grandparents themselves. They watched the saplings grow into a canopy over 25 years. Whatever is built in their place, the residents of Versova will be waiting a long time for that shade to return. “Trees are citizens of our planet, our country, our city, our landscape,” Peepal Baba says. “We need to recognise that.” Sources: ‘One old tree is worth 400 saplings – Dresden forestry expert Andreas Roloff calls for more respect for trees’ : By Dresden University of Technology, Published on 25 April 2023 ‘As urban tree shade shrinks, mortality rises-New study finds that protecting mature trees could help save lives’ : By Amanda Morris, Published on 5 August 2026 ‘BMC's Urban Forest: Miyawaki Trees In Mumbai Face Grim Fate’ : By RUCHA KANOLKAR, Published on 22 March 2024

items.title: In This Ladakh Village, Families Stay Up at Night Guarding Water So Every Farmer Gets Their Share
items.blurb: Before dawn, a farmer in Phey may be waiting for a turn that belongs to a carefully watched village schedule. Water is not taken whenever someone needs it. Its flow is shared through rules, turns, and people tasked with ensuring nobody takes more than their share. At 3,180 – 3,186 metres in Ladakh’s cold desert, this is how the community manages scarce resources through duties. A water turn is a village responsibility Phey lies west of Leh town. Its irrigation story begins beyond its fields. The village shares a stream with upstream Phyang. Winter snowfall and spring weather influence when meltwater arrives and how much reaches the channels. Springs also feed ponds that supply some fields, while upper fields rely more heavily on the stream arriving from Phyang. The water’s arrival is tied to the thaw, so a poor winter or cool spring can affect sowing and irrigation. A study by Dorjey Angchok, Tsering Stobdan and Shashi B Singh, using 1981 village-directory data, gives Phey 33 households and 176 people. It records household-based water distribution, rather than a channel-based rota, because the settlement was relatively small. These are historical figures, not a current population count. Two broken stones, one shared promise: in Ladakh, even a water rota has its own security system. Photograph: ( Wikipedia ) The chhur-pon, literally the “water lord”, coordinates irrigation. The supervisor knows which field gets water, when and in what order. In Phey, the role works alongside a rota for guarding the main water-control point. Households take turns sending people to watch the main sluice, or yur-go, that controls the main channel. Two people from each household are selected in rotation to check for blockages, overflow, or damage. When water is scarce, some must keep watch at night. The village devised a way to verify that guards reached the control point. Each person breaks a stone in two, leaves one half at the sluice and carries the other to the next person on duty. The next guard checks whether the two pieces fit, making the rota accountable without a written register. Rules also extend beyond the village boundary. Under a customary agreement known as the bandabas, Phey’s share of stream water from Phyang is protected from late evening until early morning during periods of scarcity after 21 June. It is one example of the traditional water systems of India that combine infrastructure with community rules. Who watches the cattle? Water is not the only resource that needs protecting. During the growing season, livestock straying into cultivated fields can destroy crops. Across Ladakh, the lorapa traditionally monitors free-grazing animals and prevents them from entering fields. Research documents this role as a regional institution; it does not establish that every village, including Phey today, follows it unchanged. The village has its own cattle jail, where wandering livestock learn that trespassing comes at a price. Photograph: ( Tricycle: The buddhist Review ) An animal found grazing where it should not can be taken to a lora, an enclosed cattle pound or cattle jail. Its owner must pay the penalty set under community rules to get it back. This makes each household responsible for protecting a neighbour’s crops. The lorapa is generally selected for the cropping season, with duties and penalties agreed by the community. The goba, or village head, oversees village affairs, resolves disputes and coordinates these roles. Together, they form a local system of checks and responsibilities rather than one office doing everything. A system under pressure These arrangements developed in a landscape where farming depends on short growing seasons, limited cultivable land, and water from snow and ice. The region’s wider water crisis makes fair access all the more consequential. Ladakh’s ice stupas and community-built artificial glaciers are other examples of adapting water storage and distribution to these constraints. Here, guarding water is a shared responsibility, and even the smallest shortcut can leave a neighbour short. Photograph: ( Kashmir Observer ) But customary governance is not frozen in time. Research published in 2023 and 2025 describes pressures on Ladakh’s agropastoral systems, including tourism, new livelihoods, changing livestock patterns, fencing, and the overlap between traditional institutions and formal Panchayati Raj structures. The goba’s authority has weakened in some places, while fewer people may be available for seasonal duties such as the lorapa’s. It depends on people continuing to participate, accepting shared rules and trusting others to do their turn. In Phey, even the stone-checking method shows how cooperation is reinforced by practical ways to discourage shortcuts. A government outreach camp in Phey in November 2025 also recorded residents raising concerns about water scarcity, roads, school facilities and connectivity. Traditional institutions do not replace public services or remove the need for investment. They show how a village can organise the resources and responsibilities closest to home. At this altitude, the rota is more than a timetable: shared resources depend on people keeping their word. Sources ' Community-Based Irrigation Water Management in Ladakh: A High Altitude Cold Arid Region ': by Dorjey Angchok, Tsering Stobdan and Shashi B Singh, published in the 2008 proceedings of the 12th Biannual Conference on CPR Management. ' Mountain Agropastoralism: Traditional Practices, Institutions and Pressures in the Indian Trans-Himalaya of Ladakh ': by Padma Ladon, Marcus Nüsser and Satish Chandra Garkoti for Pastoralism, published on 20 November 2023. ' Eroding Pillars: The Status of Local Institutions in Resource Management in Leh ': by Padma Ladon for the Centre of Excellence for Himalayan Studies, Shiv Nadar University, published in May 2025 ' Changing Hydrosocial Relations in the Era of Climate Change: The Case of Water Governance and New Technologies in Ladakh's Cryosphere ': by Sahana Subramanian and Mine Islar for Global Sustainability, Cambridge University Press, published in 2026 ' Mimang-Si-Sjabstogs: Administration at Your Doorstep Held at Phey Village ': by Reach Ladakh Correspondent for Reach Ladakh, published on 18 November 2025
