Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration.

Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov.

Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters.

It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity.

items.title: The census provides a critical snapshot of the US. Proposed changes could affect who is counted in 2030
items.blurb:
Trump administration’s bid to cut question on race and add one on citizenship could reshape how the US population is understood

Just a few years away from the 2030 census, the US Census Bureau is considering changes that could fundamentally reshape how people are counted – and therefore impact democracy, education, infrastructure and health. The proposed rule changes would add two new parts to the regulations that govern the census: One change would remove a question about race and ethnicity, while another would add a citizenship question. Also among the proposed changes is a line that would formally bar questions about sexual orientation from being included.

The US census is critical in understanding the American population. It helps researchers understand health and social outcomes and gives legislators the data they use for legislative redistricting and congressional apportionment. But this sweeping census rule change, quietly proposed by the Trump administration before the midterm elections, could reshape US society as we know it, warn some civil rights advocates.

items.blurb:
Another day and, despite all the promises, another damning report on the Met. There will be a reset: the public won’t be brushed off any more and neither will I

In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree.

Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most.

items.title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew
items.blurb:
Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back

Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television?

Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis.

Jonathan Liew is a sportswriter and Opinion columnist for the Guardian

items.title: Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse
items.blurb:
PM brings forward changes to non-disclosure agreements and promises consultation on staggered age of consent

  • Men have used wealth and fame to get away with abuse. No longer

Andy Burnham has called recent high-profile rape trials a “watershed moment” for the UK and has opened the door to a wider ban on non-disclosure agreements.

The prime minister has brought forward changes to NDAs so that from January victims of crimes or workplace harassment will have complete freedom over who they can speak to, even if they have signed an NDA, and he promised the move was “just the start” of a crackdown.

Continue reading...

items.title: Men have used wealth and fame to get away with abuse. No longer | Andy Burnham
items.blurb:
The NDAs that enforce silence, the behaviour that exploits the age of consent. I'll address both with sweeping changes to keep women and girls safe

  • Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse

Powerful men using their fame and money to silence anyone who calls out their behaviour. Victims treated as though they’re the ones who’ve done something wrong. And a culture where abuse can hide in plain sight because people in positions of power think they can get away with it. That’s what we’ve seen in the past few weeks. This must be a watershed moment. Not just for the culture of the entertainment industry but for us as a nation.

Things have improved in the past decade or so, but we are still far from being where we need to be for women and girls to feel safe and be safe. Sadly, many women and girls will find the stories of the past few weeks all too close to home, whether it’s casual disrespect in the workplace, undermining “jokes”, or being told they are somehow at fault for something that has happened to them.

Continue reading...

Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s defense minister said after the Pentagon released a scathing memo that criticized the supposedly “atrophied” defence capabilities of its northern neighbour.

items.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
items.blurb:
Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life

Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing.

Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.”

Continue reading...

items.title: Once ‘capital of the Confederacy’, Virginia enshrines rights to voting, abortion and gay marriage
items.blurb:
Organizers won key civil liberties protections on election day – and women and Black advocates were at the forefront

Progressives made historic gains in the south during the midterm elections – and Virginia was no exception. The state approved three constitutional amendments protecting civil liberties that have eroded in Trump’s second term: enshrining the rights to abortion and same-sex marriage, and restoring voting rights to those with past felony convictions.

These victories were led by women and Black organizers who say they want to capitalize on the momentum and advocate for policies that expand the protections they secured on election day.
